russia.name: Russian Empire
russia.note: Includes the imperial army's last garrisons in Iran, which stayed through the revolutions of 1917 and withdrew in early 1918.

qawasim.name: Qasimi shaykhdoms of Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah

jk_komala.name: Society for the Revival of Kurdistan

tangestan.name: Khans of Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti

baluch_bampur.name: Baluch sardars of Bampur and Saravan

makran_baluch.name: Gichki and Baluch sardars of Makran

jangali.name: Jangal movement and Gilan Soviet Republic
jangali.name_fa: نهضت جنگل و جمهوری شوروی گیلان

urmia_1918.name: Assyrian and Armenian forces at Urmia

turkey.name: Turkey
turkey.note: Ankara government from November 1922; republic proclaimed 29 Oct 1923.

kartli_kakheti.name: Kartli-Kakheti (eastern Georgia, incl. Borchali, Kazakh-Shamshadil, Lori)
kartli_kakheti.geometry_note: Modern Kakheti, Kvemo Kartli, Tbilisi, Shida Kartli, Mtskheta-Mtianeti, plus the Muslim-ruled marches that were in the Georgian king's orbit in 1800 (Qazakh/Agstafa/Tovuz = Kazakh-Shamshadil sultanates; Armenian Tavush and Lori). Samtskhe-Javakheti (Ottoman Akhaltsikhe pashalik), Imereti, Guria, Samegrelo and Abkhazia are excluded: no Tehran claim found, although Gulistan Art. 3 names them. Frontier zone: borders of the marches are approximate. Gulistan Art. II line runs 'along the boundary separating Iravan khanate from Yelizavetpol district, Gazakh and Shamsaddin lands... the chain of Pambak mountains - the boundary of Shuragol - Arpachay', so Qazakh/Shamshadil (Qazakh, Agstafa, Tovuz), Lori/Pambak and Shuragol lay on the ceded side; Lori and Tavush stay as marches of the Georgian king.

shuragel_shirak.name: Shuragel (Shirak plain, Gyumri area)
shuragel_shirak.geometry_note: Modern Shirak province. Shuragel/Shoragol was a Muslim sultanate on the Georgian-Erivan frontier; its exact extent is uncertain.

ganja_khanate.name: Ganja Khanate
ganja_khanate.geometry_note: Ganja city and surrounding districts (Goranboy, Goygol, Shamkir, Dashkasan, Gadabay, Samukh, Naftalan). Pre-1880 frontier zone: khanate limits fluid; Qazakh and Shamshadil are mapped with Kartli-Kakheti.

karabakh_khanate.name: Karabakh Khanate (excluding Shusha), incl. Zangezur
karabakh_khanate.geometry_note: Lowland and highland Karabakh plus Zangezur (Syunik); Shusha is a separate region so that the 1826 hold-out can be shown. Frontier zone; khanate edges (esp. Zangezur/Meghri and the Kura lowlands) are approximate.

shusha.name: Shusha (fortress and district)
shusha.geometry_note: Shusha city + Shusha district: Karabakh's capital, held by a Russian garrison and Armenian defenders through the 1826 Persian siege.

shaki_khanate.name: Shaki Khanate
shaki_khanate.geometry_note: Shaki city and district, Qabala and Oghuz. Qakh/Zaqatala/Balakan (Elisu sultanate, Jar-Belokan) are NOT mapped: only nominal Safavid-era overlordship found, no distinct Qajar claim.

shirvan_khanate.name: Shirvan Khanate (incl. Salyan lowlands)
shirvan_khanate.geometry_note: Shamakhi, Agsu, Ismailli, Gobustan and the Kura-Aras lowlands (Hajigabul to Salyan/Neftchala). Khanate had 17 mahals; boundaries with Quba, Baku and Mughan are approximate.

baku_khanate.name: Baku Khanate
baku_khanate.geometry_note: Baku city, Absheron peninsula and Sumqayit.

quba_khanate.name: Quba Khanate
quba_khanate.geometry_note: Quba, Qusar, Khachmaz, Khizi, Shabran, Siazan. Quba and Derbent were united under Shaykh Ali Khan 1802-06.

derbent_khanate.name: Derbent Khanate (Derbent coast, southern Dagestan)
derbent_khanate.geometry_note: Derbent city and district plus Magaramkent and Suleyman-Stalsky; the khanate was a narrow coastal strip.

south_dagestan.name: Southern Dagestan (Tabasaran, Kaytag, Kura, Akhty, Rutul)
south_dagestan.geometry_note: Highland districts south of the Shamkhal/Avar lands. Extent of Tehran's nominal claim is poorly defined; Chechnya and northern Dagestan were never claimed. Gulistan Art. III names 'Dagestan' among the lands Persia recognised as Russian, which is the only documentary basis for a Persian claim; extent unsourced, kept low.

talysh_lankaran.name: Talysh Khanate, northern part ceded at Gulistan (Lankaran, Astara-north, Masally, Mughan lowlands)
talysh_lankaran.geometry_note: Split of the Talysh khanate: Gulistan gave Russia 'the greater part of Talysh north of the Astara river' and 'the better part of Moghan'; the remainder (Zuvand highlands) went in 1828. Districts allocated to each cession are approximate; the 1813-18 delimitation commission fixed the real line. Gulistan Art. II fixed the Mughan line 'Adinabazar - straight through Mugan lowland - Yeddibulag passage - Aras' (Turkmenchay Art. IV repeats the same Yeddibulag-Mugan-Bolgarchay-Adinabazar line, so the Mughan share was already Russian in 1813) and left the Talysh frontier 'at Zinzeley and Ardabil' to commissioners (completed 1818). A 2013 Russian review says the southern Talysh 'together with Astara' stayed Persian until 1828, so Astara district may belong with the Persian remainder in 1813-28; it is shown here with the 1813 cession, at low confidence.

talysh_zuvand.name: Talysh Khanate remainder (Zuvand highlands) ceded at Turkmenchay
talysh_zuvand.geometry_note: Lerik and Yardymli (Zuvand). Turkmenchay Art. 4 draws the line 'along the mountain chain separating Zuvand and Arsh'. Which districts were Persian between 1813 and 1828 is approximate.

erivan_khanate.name: Erivan Khanate (incl. Surmali/Igdir, Sharur-Daralayaz)
erivan_khanate.geometry_note: Yerevan, Ararat, Armavir, Kotayk and Aragatsotn plains plus Igdir (Surmali) and the Sharur-Sadarak lowlands. Gokcha/Sevan (Gegharkunik) is a separate region; Vayots Dzor is with Nakhchivan; Lori/Shirak with Georgia. Approximate mahal limits.

gokcha_sevan.name: Gokcha / Lake Sevan zone (Gegharkunik)
gokcha_sevan.geometry_note: Modern Gegharkunik. The northern shore was seized by Russia in 1825 on the argument that Gulistan's vague frontier gave it the district.

nakhchivan_khanate.name: Nakhchivan Khanate (Nakhchivan, Julfa, Vayots Dzor)
nakhchivan_khanate.geometry_note: Modern Nakhchivan districts except Ordubad (separate) and Sharur/Sadarak (Erivan), plus Vayots Dzor, which Wikipedia attributes to the khanate.

ordubad.name: Ordubad
ordubad.geometry_note: Ordubad district, on the Aras; part of the Nakhchivan khanate but occupied separately.

abbasabad_bridgehead.name: Abbasabad bridgehead (right bank of the Aras)
abbasabad_bridgehead.geometry_note: Tiny parcel inside modern Iran. Treaty of Turkmenchay Art. IV: a circle of 3 Russian half-versts (1.5 versts) radius 'around the fortification of the tower on the right bank of Araz' (IBS 25: bridgehead on the right bank opposite the fort). Iranica (Ekbal, 'Abbasabad'): fort built 1810 by Abbas Mirza on the northern bank at Yazdabad, ~6 miles SW of Nakhchivan. Centre (39.073N 45.403E) taken at the Aras dam/reservoir; true position uncertain by several km.

firuzeh_firyuza.name: Firuzeh (Firyuza oasis and district, Kopet Dag)
firuzeh_firyuza.geometry_note: Oasis and adjacent district ceded in 1893. Centre approximate; radius is illustrative (district area not found). NOT the Firuzeh county of Razavi Khorasan. EB 1911 describes the 1893 cession as 'the small but very fertile district of Firuza and the adjacent lands between Baba Durmaz and Lutfabad' (Persia received the village of Hissar and 'a strip of desert ground near Abbasabad' in exchange) and the 1921 Moscow treaty speaks of 'the village of Firouzeh and the adjacent land'; the ceded district was therefore probably a strip of the Kopet Dag foothills rather than a 9 km disc. The disc is illustrative only.

turkmen_akhal_tejen.name: Akhal-Atek oases and Tejen (Turkmen lands under the Kopet Dag)
turkmen_akhal_tejen.geometry_note: Gokdepe, Ak Bugday, Baherden, Kaka (Abivard), Babadayhan and Tejen: the Tekke oases whose overlordship Tehran claimed until 1881. The Iranica phrase is 'lands beyond the Tejen... Meyhana, Abivard, Nesa and Marv'.

old_sarakhs_north.name: Old Sarakhs (Serakhs, north/east bank)
old_sarakhs_north.geometry_note: Serakhs district across the Hari Rud from Iranian Sarakhs.

bayezid.name: Bayezid / Toprakkale district (Ottoman, held by Iran 1821-23)
bayezid.geometry_note: Dogubayazit (Bayezid), Diyadin, Caldiran, Eleskirt (Toprakkale); the extent of Abbas Mirza's occupation is approximate.

baban_sulaymaniyah.name: Baban emirate / Shahrizor (Sulaymaniyah)
baban_sulaymaniyah.geometry_note: Modern Sulaymaniyah governorate as proxy for the Baban principality (Sulaymaniyah, Shahrizor, Qara Dagh); real extent shifted.

zohab_lowlands.name: Zohab lowlands (west), around Khanaqin
zohab_lowlands.geometry_note: Khanaqin district as proxy for the 'lowlands in the western part of the province of Zohab' ceded in 1847. The 1847 text gives no coordinates; the line was fixed by the 1913-14 commission.

zohab_transferred.name: Zohab 'Transferred Territory' (1913)
zohab_transferred.geometry_note: Location and extent are uncertain. Sources say Persia evacuated a 'Transferred Territory' in the Zohab sector under the 1913 Protocol (Anglo-Persian Oil Co. rights safeguarded), the area around Qasr-e Shirin/Naft Khaneh east of the Sirwan; Qasr-e Shirin town stayed Persian.

kotur_zone.name: Kotur-neighbourhood strip ceded to Turkey in 1932
kotur_zone.geometry_note: Iranica (Schofield): the 1932 line left Turkey 'an additional ninety square miles in the neighbourhood of Kotur' (between Guirberan and Kuch Dagh). CONFLICT: IBS 28 and Mojtahed-Zadeh (via Wikipedia) say the Qotur change was in Iran's favour; Iranica's specific, detailed account is followed (low confidence). Polygon is a strip along the present border on the Turkish side (units Saray, Ozalp).

little_ararat_zone.name: Little Ararat zone ceded to Turkey in 1932
little_ararat_zone.geometry_note: 1932: 'the whole of Lesser Ararat' passed to Turkey (~60 sq mi, the Northern Zone). Polygon is a strip along the present gb border on the Turkish side (units Dogubayazit, Aralik, Igdir).

muhammarah_khizr.name: Muhammarah (Khorramshahr) and Khizr island (Abadan)
muhammarah_khizr.geometry_note: Inside modern Iran. Mapped separately because its sovereignty was disputed with the Ottomans before 1847. The autonomy of the Ka'b and Muhaysin sheikhs is shown in its own records.

shatt_east_half.name: Shatt al-Arab (Arvand Rud), eastern half-channel, Khaiin canal to the sea
shatt_east_half.geometry_note: The river is an international boundary river; the thalweg (median line of the main navigable channel) was agreed in 1975. Strip is schematic.

shatt_muhammara_anchorage.name: Muhammarah anchorage reach (Khaiin canal to the Karun mouth)
shatt_muhammara_anchorage.geometry_note: 'The modern port and anchorage of Muhammara, above and below the junction of the river Karun with the Shatt al-Arab' (1913 Protocol); extent of the reach is approximate.

shatt_abadan_thalweg.name: Shatt al-Arab opposite Abadan (thalweg segment of 1937)
shatt_abadan_thalweg.geometry_note: Segment where the 1937 treaty moved the boundary from the Iranian low-water mark to the thalweg.

irq_majnoon.name: Majnoon Islands (Hawizeh marshes)
irq_majnoon.geometry_note: Operation Kheibar captured ~160 km2 with ~50 oil wells.

irq_halabja.name: Halabja district (Iraqi Kurdistan)
irq_halabja.geometry_note: Halabcha district; Operation Dawn 10 also took Dojileh and Khurmal.

herat_state.name: Herat and Farah (Herat principality)
herat_state.geometry_note: Modern Herat and Farah provinces as the Sadozai principality and its dependencies (Ghurian, Sabzawar/Shindand, Lash-Juwayn). Ghurian was not split out: no reliable separate chronology found.

sistan_afghan.name: Afghan Sistan (Nimruz: Chakhansur, Kang, Zaranj)
sistan_afghan.geometry_note: Modern Nimruz province (Goldsmid's 'Outer Seistan', the right/east bank of the Helmand and lands beyond).

makran_kech_panjgur.name: Kech and Panjgur (Makran)
makran_kech_panjgur.geometry_note: Modern Kech and Panjgur districts: the Gichki/Kalat lands assigned to Kalat by the 1871 Goldsmid line (Panjgur, Parum, Buleda, Mand, Tump, Kech, Dasht). Gwadar (Omani) not mapped.

kuhak.name: Kuhak district
kuhak.geometry_note: Small district awarded to Kalat in 1871, reclaimed by Iran, occupied May 1874, formally Iranian in 1896. Radius illustrative.

mirjaveh.name: Mirjaveh frontier parcel
mirjaveh.geometry_note: Disputed 1896-1905 between the Holdich line's 'blue' reading and Persian possession; radius illustrative.

chabahar.name: Chabahar (Omani appanage)
chabahar.geometry_note: Inside modern Iran; included because it was a Muscat/Omani possession.

sirri.name: Sirri island
sirri.geometry_note: Inside modern Iran; parcel because the Qasimi deputy-governors of Lengeh held it.

mashhad_area.name: Mashhad district (Nader Mirza 1796-1803; Salar revolt 1848-50)
mashhad_area.geometry_note: Mashhad county plus Binalud. Nader Mirza and Hasan Khan Salar each held the shrine city; neither man's wider reach is mappable to counties (see the wider Khorasan region of Salar's revolt). Modern Mashhad county is far larger than the 19th-century city+oasis.

salar_khorasan_wide.name: Sabzevar-Neyshabur zone held by Hasan Khan Salar (1848-49)
salar_khorasan_wide.geometry_note: Sources only name Sabzevar and Neyshabur (Nishapur) as retaken by the government in March 1849; the neighbouring counties are inferred. Wikipedia also lists Bojnurd and Qa'en as dominated by Salar; those are mapped as separate regions (Bojnurd and the Qa'enat).

torbat_qarai.name: Torbat-e Heydarieh (Qara'i principality)
torbat_qarai.geometry_note: Iranica: a Qara'i principality "stretching from the gates of Mashhad to Khaf" with Torbat-e Heydarieh as capital. Counties are an approximation of that corridor; the real boundary fluctuated with the chiefs' power.

quchan_zafaranlu.name: Quchan (Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanate)
quchan_zafaranlu.geometry_note: Za'faranlu Kurds held Quchan/Chenaran (Iranica names Chenaran as their seat in the Qajar period). Faruj and Dargaz are approximations of their pastoral range on the Atrek/Kopet-Dag side.

bojnurd_shadlu.name: Bojnurd-Esfarayen (Shadlu Kurdish ilkhanate)
bojnurd_shadlu.geometry_note: Iranica: Shadlu controlled Esfarayen and Bojnurd; Kurds of other tribes (Keyvanlu, Bicaranlu, Zangalanlu...) held the remainder of northern Khorasan. Counties are the modern North Khorasan block minus Quchan-side units.

qaenat_alam.name: Qa'enat (Khozeimeh/'Alam amirate)
qaenat_alam.geometry_note: Core Qa'enat districts of modern South Khorasan. Tabas/Ferdows/Boshruyeh were at times attached to the Qa'enat governorship but are left out. Sistan is mapped separately.

tabas_khans.name: Tabas (hereditary Zangu'i/Vakil khans)
tabas_khans.geometry_note: Tabas county only; the historical Tabas-e Masina/Gilaki governorship may have reached Ferdows/Boshruyeh margins, not mapped.

sistan.name: Sistan (Persian Sistan)
sistan.geometry_note: Modern Iranian Sistan = the 1872 Goldsmid award line (west of the Helmand). Before 1872 the Sistan lowlands were ruled by local chiefs and disputed with Afghanistan; the Iranian county set is only the part that ended up in Iran.

baluch_bampur_saravan.name: Persian Baluchistan: Bampur, Fahraj, Sarbaz, Dizzak, Saravan
baluch_bampur_saravan.name_fa: بلوچستان (بمپور، فهرج، سرباز، دیزک و سراوان)
baluch_bampur_saravan.geometry_note: Western/central Baluchistan, the domain of the Bampur governorate and the Barakzai (Baranzai) chiefs. Counties approximate old districts Bampur, Dizzak, Sarbaz, Geh and Qasr-e Qand named by Iranica.

baluch_sarhad.name: Sarhad (Khash, Mirjaveh, Zahedan/Dozdab)
baluch_sarhad.geometry_note: Northern Baluch highland (Sarhad) along the British Baluchistan frontier; the Dozdab (Zahedan) railhead lies in Zahedan county. Boundary with the Bampur block approximate.

chabahar_oman.name: Chabahar bay (Omani dependency until 1872)
chabahar_oman.geometry_note: Only the Chabahar-Dashtiari coast was concerned. The two modern counties are much larger than the Omani-claimed bay and its Jadgal-controlled hinterland.

pesyan_khorasan.name: Khorasan under Col. Pesyan (1921)
pesyan_khorasan.geometry_note: Razavi Khorasan minus the Quchan/Dargaz Kurdish zone (which fought Pesyan). Wikipedia calls the entity the Autonomous Government of Khorasan with Mashhad as capital; actual reach beyond Mashhad, Neyshabur and Sabzevar is poorly documented.

turkmen_sahra.name: Turkmen Sahra (Yomut and Goklen)
turkmen_sahra.geometry_note: Plain between the Atrek, the Caspian shore and the Gorgan river. Yomut lived west/south of Gonbad, Goklen to the east; Galikash/Minudasht/Azadshahr were mixed or Persian-settled and are omitted. Tribal ranges were seasonal and fuzzy.

shahsevan.name: Shahsevan country (Ardabil, Moghan, Sabalan)
shahsevan.geometry_note: Winter pastures in Moghan (Parsabad, Bilehsavar, Garmi) and summer pastures on the Sabalan slopes (Meshkinshahr, Ardebil, Khalkhal) = modern Ardabil Province. Shahsevan also ranged into Sarab (East Azerbaijan; left out to avoid overlap with Azadistan) and, per Iranica, between Zanjan and Qazvin; only the core block is mapped.

gilan.name: Gilan
gilan.geometry_note: Whole of modern Gilan province. Jangali control (1915-20) was concentrated in Fuman, Shaft, Siahkal, Rasht hinterland, Lahijan and Rudbar; the coast (Anzali, Rasht) was repeatedly held by Russian/British garrisons or the Soviets, so single-province treatment is a simplification.

tabriz_area.name: Tabriz and the Jolfa road
tabriz_area.geometry_note: Russian garrisons held Tabriz and the Julfa-Tabriz axis; the 1908-09 siege concerned the Tabriz city and its quarters. Modern Tabriz county is larger than the 1909 city.

azadistan_khiabani.name: Azadistan (Khiabani) - East Azerbaijan
azadistan_khiabani.geometry_note: Khiabani's movement claimed the whole province of Azerbaijan; Iranica says only a few towns stayed under Tehran or tribal chiefs, but only Tabriz's control is firmly documented. East Azerbaijan is used as the maximum plausible extent.

urmia_khoy_salmas.name: Urmia-Khoy-Salmas plain
urmia_khoy_salmas.geometry_note: Counties around Lake Urmia's west shore that saw the Russian withdrawal (1918), the Assyrian-Kurdish war and the Ottoman reoccupation (June-July 1918).

ottoman_border_strip_1906.name: Ottoman-occupied frontier strip west of Lake Urmia (1906-12)
ottoman_border_strip_1906.geometry_note: Schematic strip about 25-40 km wide along the border. Whole counties would greatly overstate the occupation.

russian_occupation_azerbaijan_1827.name: Azerbaijan occupied by Russia (1827-28) except Khoy
russian_occupation_azerbaijan_1827.geometry_note: Tabriz (13 Oct 1827), Urmia (28 Jan 1828), Ardabil (8 Feb 1828) are the documented captures; Marand/Jolfa (the Aras crossing and road), Khoy and Salmas are inferred as lying on the Russian line. The Turkmenchay treaty tied evacuation to indemnity instalments, so the occupied area shrank by stages. Khoy is mapped separately because Russia kept it as security for the indemnity long after the rest of Azerbaijan was evacuated.

qazvin_zanjan_norperforce.name: Qazvin-Zanjan sector of Norperforce
qazvin_zanjan_norperforce.geometry_note: Norperforce had its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil (Gilan), a battalion at Zanjan and posts along the Manjil-Qazvin road. The occupation was a road-line, not a full area.

sanandaj_zone.name: Sanandaj / Ardalan Kurdistan (and southern Kurdistan in 1979-83)
sanandaj_zone.geometry_note: Modern Kurdistan Province. The Ardalan vilayet centred on Sanandaj (Senneh) and Bijar, Kamyaran, Marivan, Sarvabad; Saqqez and Baneh were Mukri/Ardalan marchland and are the least certain inclusions for 1800-67.

kurdistan_kermanshah_border_1979.name: Paveh-Javanrud-Ravansar (Kermanshah Kurdistan, 1979-83)
kurdistan_kermanshah_border_1979.geometry_note: Kurdish-majority counties of Kermanshah province in which Kurdish forces took garrisons in March 1979 and fought in Aug-Sept 1979.

mahabad_zone.name: Mahabad zone (Mukriyan; Republic of Mahabad; KDPI core)
mahabad_zone.geometry_note: Mukriyan = south of Lake Urmia incl. Mahabad, Bukan, Sardasht, Oshnaviyeh. The 1946 republic is usually described as Mahabad, Bukan, Naghadeh, Piranshahr, Oshnavieh, with Sardasht often added. Miandoab was Azeri-majority and contested; it is left out here and put under ADP.

ubeydullah_1880.name: Area overrun by Sheikh Ubeydullah (1880)
ubeydullah_1880.name_fa: مناطق تصرف‌شده به دست شیخ عبیدالله (۱۲۵۹)
ubeydullah_1880.geometry_note: Sources say Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh were taken and Urmia held out; Miandoab lies between them. Raiding extended widely west of Lake Urmia, but held ground is not mappable.

simko_core.name: Shikak country (Simko), Salmas-Chehriq-Ushnu
simko_core.geometry_note: Chehriq fortress (Salmas county) was Simko's base; Qotur/Baradost/Ushnu and the Mamash/Mangur/Piran pastures are covered by the neighbouring counties. Extent varied month to month.

simko_extended.name: Mahabad-Miandoab sector under Simko (1921-22)
simko_extended.name_fa: مهاباد، بوکان و میاندوآب در دورهٔ سمیتقو
simko_extended.geometry_note: Wikipedia (single source) credits Simko with Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) from Oct 1921; control of Miandoab/Naghadeh is less certain.

kalhor_border_kurds.name: Kalhor-Guran-Sanjabi border Kurds (Kermanshah frontier)
kalhor_border_kurds.geometry_note: Iranica: under Davud Khan Kalhor "absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border", also subjecting Guran and Sanjabi. Counties approximate this border belt.

kermanshah_area.name: Kermanshah plain and Hamadan road (Kermanshah, Sahneh, Harsin, Kangavar, Sonqor)
kermanshah_area.geometry_note: Core Kermanshah-Sahneh-Bisotun-Harsin corridor that Russian, Ottoman and British forces fought over in 1915-18; the border-belt counties (Qasr-e Shirin etc.) are mapped with the Kalhor border region.

hamadan_area.name: Hamadan province
hamadan_area.geometry_note: Modern Hamadan province; Hamadan city and the Hamadan-Kermanshah and Hamadan-Qazvin roads are what was occupied.

luristan_pish_e_kuh.name: Luristan (Pish-e Kuh)
luristan_pish_e_kuh.geometry_note: Modern Lorestan province. The Pish-e Kuh Lur tribes (Bala Gariveh, Dirakvand, Silakhor, Selseleh, Bayravand...) ranged over this block; the towns of Khorramabad and Borujerd had Qajar governors but the highlands did not obey them.

pusht_e_kuh.name: Pusht-e Kuh (Ilam; walis)
pusht_e_kuh.geometry_note: Iranica lists Ayvan, Sirvan-Chardavol, Ilam, Darreh Shahr, Mehran and Abdanan as Pusht-e Kuh, with Dehloran sometimes included.

bakhtiari.name: Bakhtiari country (Chahar Mahal and eastern Khuzestan)
bakhtiari.geometry_note: Summer quarters (yaylaq) in Chahar Mahal and the Zagros crest, winter quarters (qeshlaq) in the Khuzestan piedmont (Masjed Soleyman, Izeh, Lali, Andika, Baghmalek). Fereydan/Fereydunshahr and Semirom fringes and the Khuzestan lowland ranges are excluded.

kohgiluyeh_boirahmad.name: Kohgiluyeh, Boir Ahmad and Mamasani
kohgiluyeh_boirahmad.geometry_note: Six tribal groups of Kuhgiluya; Boir Ahmad is the largest. Mamasani/Rostam (Fars) joined them under Emamqoli Khan against Reza Shah. The lowland market town Behbahan (Khuzestan) and the Gachsaran/Dogonbadan piedmont fringe are only partly covered; Behbahan is deliberately left out to avoid overlap with the Khuzestan occupation block.

qashqai.name: Qashqai range (Fars)
qashqai.geometry_note: Qashqai winter quarters in Firuzabad, Farashband, Kazerun and the Gulf-side Qir/Karzin; summer quarters round Semirom, Eqlid, Abadeh and Sepidan. Migration routes crossed Shiraz county. The range was seasonal and overlapped other tribes (Khamseh, Mamasani).

mohammerah_core.name: Mohammerah (Khorramshahr) and Abadan island
mohammerah_core.geometry_note: Seat of the Muhaysin/Ka'b sheikhs. Modern county boundaries are larger than the 19th-century sheikhdom nucleus.

khuzestan_fallahiyeh.name: Fallahiyeh (Shadegan), Hendijan, Mahshahr, Ramshir
khuzestan_fallahiyeh.geometry_note: The Ka'b heartland (Fallahiyeh=Shadegan) and the Khaz'al estates granted in 1903 (Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla, Mashur).

khuzestan_khazal_ext.name: Northern Khuzestan placed under Khaz'al (1907-24)
khuzestan_khazal_ext.name_fa: شمال خوزستان در قلمرو شیخ خزعل
khuzestan_khazal_ext.geometry_note: Iranica: from 1907 Khaz'al administered northern Khuzestan; by 1911 "most of the country" was under the sheikh except Dezful and Shushtar. Counties are inferred.

lengeh_qawasim.name: Bandar Lengeh and dependencies (Qawasim)
lengeh_qawasim.geometry_note: Port of Lengeh and its dependent coast (Charak/Mogh, in Parsian county). The Qasimi island dependencies (Abu Musa, the Tunbs, Sirri) are mapped as frontier regions.

bastak.name: Bastak (hereditary khans)
bastak.geometry_note: Hereditary Khans of Bastak governed the Bastak/Irahistan district under the governor of Fars/Lar.

larestan.name: Larestan (Lar, Gerash, Evaz, Khonj)
larestan.geometry_note: Area ruled by Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari 1909-15; extent between Lar town, Gerash, Khonj and Lamerd inferred from contemporary descriptions.

tangestan_dashtestan.name: Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Bushehr hinterland)
tangestan_dashtestan.geometry_note: Tribal districts behind Bushehr; khans of Tangestan (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah), Dashtestan and Dashti are the actors.

bushehr.name: Bushehr port and county
bushehr.geometry_note: Bushehr county includes the port, Reshire and, administratively, Kharg island; Kharg has its own circle region.

kharg.name: Kharg island
kharg.geometry_note: Small island; circle approximates its outline.

basidu.name: Basidu (west tip of Qeshm island)
basidu.geometry_note: Station and depot at the west end of Qeshm; British claims never covered the whole island.

ashurada.name: Ashurada island (Gorgan Bay)
ashurada.geometry_note: Small island group; circle approximates it.

omani_lease_bandar_abbas.name: Bandar Abbas, Minab-Khamir coast, Qeshm and Hormuz (Omani lease)
omani_lease_bandar_abbas.name_fa: بندرعباس، میناب، خمیر، قشم و هرمز (اجارهٔ عمان)
omani_lease_bandar_abbas.geometry_note: Iranica: a coastal strip of about 150 km from Minab in the east to Khamir in the west, plus the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz, and inland about 30 miles in some British accounts. County units over-extend inland; Hormuz is inside Bandar-e Abbas county.

spr_garrison_towns.name: South Persia Rifles base at Bandar Abbas (1916-21)
spr_garrison_towns.geometry_note: Circle approximation only. Sykes landed at Bandar Abbas in March 1916, reached Kerman on 12 June 1916 and Shiraz on 11 Nov 1916; Kerman and Shiraz are mapped separately.

isfahan_1909.name: Isfahan (Bakhtiari constitutionalists, 1909)
isfahan_1909.geometry_note: Isfahan city and the surrounding county.

iraq_khorramshahr.name: Khorramshahr (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
iraq_khorramshahr.geometry_note: The Iraqi bridgehead covered the city and the eastern bank of the Shatt; the whole county is shown.

iraq_abadan.name: Abadan island (siege 1980-81)
iraq_abadan.geometry_note: Abadan was besieged but the city and refinery stayed in Iranian hands; Iraqi forces took parts of the north/west of the island and the Bahmanshir bank.

iraq_susangerd.name: Susangerd-Bostan-Hoveyzeh plain (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
iraq_susangerd.geometry_note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of Dasht-e Azadegan; exact holdings varied (Iran liberated Bostan 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981, but Iraqi forces still held ground near Susangerd).

iraq_west_front.name: Qasr-e Shirin-Sarpol-e Zahab-Gilan-e Gharb-Dehloran (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
iraq_west_front.name_fa: قصرشیرین، سرپل ذهاب، گیلان غرب و دهلران
iraq_west_front.geometry_note: Iraq entered 20-40 km deep on this front (Qasr-e Shirin 20 km, Dehloran 30 km according to later accounts); counties overstate the depth.

iraq_mehran.name: Mehran
iraq_mehran.geometry_note: Mehran changed hands several times (1980, 1986, 1988); the county is shown whole although the occupation was of the town and its approaches.

iraq_border_pockets.name: Iraqi-held border pockets after the 1988 ceasefire (to Aug 1990)
iraq_border_pockets.name_fa: نوار مرزی در اشغال عراق پس از آتش‌بس
iraq_border_pockets.geometry_note: Schematic strip along the border; the actual pockets were a handful of positions.

wwii_soviet_adp.name: Soviet zone of Azerbaijan (ADP area)
wwii_soviet_adp.name_fa: آذربایجان در منطقهٔ اشغال شوروی (حکومت پیشه‌وری)
wwii_soviet_adp.geometry_note: East and West Azerbaijan (minus the Mahabad-republic counties), Ardabil and Zanjan. Zanjan's inclusion in the ADP is from general accounts; the Democrats' writ in the south of the area (Zanjan, Takab, Miandoab) was thinner and was cut off by the Iranian army before reaching Tabriz.

wwii_soviet_north.name: Soviet-occupied north (Gilan, Mazandaran, Golestan, Qazvin)
wwii_soviet_north.name_fa: شمال در اشغال شوروی (گیلان، مازندران، گلستان، قزوین، سمنان)
wwii_soviet_north.geometry_note: Gilan, Mazandaran and Gorgan are named in the sources; Qazvin (southern outpost of the Soviet line) and Semnan are inferred. Soviet garrisons were concentrated in towns and along the roads; Iranian civil administration continued. Semnan province is mapped separately because the Soviets left Mashhad, Shahrud and Semnan in March 1946, earlier than the rest.

wwii_soviet_khorasan.name: Soviet-occupied Khorasan (1941-43)
wwii_soviet_khorasan.geometry_note: Iranica: Soviet troops took Mashhad and Bojnurd and "occupied all of Khorasan" until winter 1943; the south (Birjand etc.) is not included.

wwii_british_zone.name: British-occupied south and west (1941-46)
wwii_british_zone.name_fa: جنوب و غرب در اشغال بریتانیا
wwii_british_zone.geometry_note: The British entered Khuzestan, Kermanshah and Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941 and held the Persian Corridor from the Gulf to Hamadan. Paiforce garrisons later reached Isfahan, Shiraz and the Gulf ports, but Fars (Qashqai/Khamseh range, treated separately), Hormozgan and the east are NOT included because British control there was thin or absent. Only a schematic block. Sanandaj county is included because British and Soviet columns met at Sanandaj on 30 Aug 1941 and 'southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj' fell in the British zone (low confidence; the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the zones). The wider extent of the British zone (Fars, Isfahan, Kerman, Hormozgan) is uncertain.

wwii_soviet_semnan.name: Soviet-occupied Semnan province (1941-46)
wwii_soviet_semnan.geometry_note: Semnan province counties (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan, Garmsar etc.), mapped separately from the rest of the Soviet zone. Sources say the Soviets held Shahrud and Semnan until March 1946; the extent south to Garmsar is inferred from the Soviet advance to Qazvin/Tehran and the Mashhad road.

russian_khoy_1828.name: Khoy (Russian-held pledge, 1828)
russian_khoy_1828.geometry_note: Khoy county. Under Turkmenchay Russia evacuated Azerbaijan except Khoy, which it held as a deposit until the indemnity was paid; modern Khoy county is larger than the 1828 district.

shiraz_1915.name: Shiraz (pro-German Gendarmerie, 1915-16)
shiraz_1915.geometry_note: Circle round Shiraz city; the surrounding Fars countryside was divided among Qashqai, Khamseh and Tangestani forces.

zanjan_babi_1850.name: Zanjan town (Babi revolt, 1850-51)
zanjan_babi_1850.geometry_note: Circle round Zanjan town; the divided town cannot be mapped more finely.

abadan_british_1914.name: Abadan island (British garrison, 1914-18)
abadan_british_1914.geometry_note: Abadan county stands in for the island refinery zone; the British perimeter did not cover the whole county.

spr_kerman.name: South Persia Rifles garrison at Kerman (1916-21)
spr_kerman.geometry_note: Circle approximation of the garrison town.

spr_shiraz.name: South Persia Rifles garrison at Shiraz (1916-21)
spr_shiraz.geometry_note: Circle approximation of the garrison town.

iran_core.name: Iran within its modern borders
iran_core.geometry_note: Modern Iran minus the border parcels whose status changed; those carry their own records.

Tehran treated the Georgian king as a vassal (vali) since Nader Shah/Karim Khan Zand; Agha Mohammad Khan sacked Tbilisi in Sept 1795 to enforce this. Fath-Ali Shah never recognised the Russian annexation (Dec 1800/Sept 1801), which was a casus belli in 1804. Renounced in Gulistan Art. 3 (Georgia 'with the province of Shuragel'). Claim long predates 1800; 1800 is the map baseline.

Erivan khanate/Georgian march; named in Gulistan Art. 3 ('Georgia together with the province of Shuragel') as ceded. Tehran's pre-1813 claim is inferred from this and from the 1826 Iranian recapture of 'Pambak and Shuregol' (not mapped). Gulistan Art. III lists 'Georgia (together with the province of Shuragol)' among the lands Persia recognised as Russian and Art. II's line runs 'the chain of Pambak mountains - the boundary of Shuragol - Arpachay'; Behrooz (2023) has Hosein Khan Sardar 'conquering Pambak and Shuregol in northern Erivan' on 28-30 July 1826. Raised from low to medium.
Khan Javad (Ziyadoghlu-Qajar) submitted to Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. Ceded in Gulistan Art. 3.

As Karabakh Khanate (Shusha was the khan's seat).
Under Iranian suzerainty (1743-1813); 'Shakki' named in Gulistan Art. 3.

IV draws the line 'from the peak of Qamarkuhum along the mountain chain separating Zuvand and Arsh... the region of Zuvand is joined to Russia' and from the Velgic border to the north source of the Astara river and down its bed: Zuvand (Lerik, Yardymli) was ceded in 1828 while Arsh stayed Persian.

III), and the Aras line of Art. IV put the left-bank Ordubad district in Russia (Wikipedia's summary of Art. IV lists 'the Ordubad and Mughan regions').
Persian territory; Turkmenchay Art. 4 ceded a semicircle round Abbasabad fort on the right bank.
Returned to Persia in the 1893 convention (in exchange for Firuzeh).

Left to Persia by the Akhal-Khorasan Convention (21 Dec 1881); ceded to Russia in the 1893 convention. Persia probably claimed it earlier (not documented). EB 1911: in June 1893 Persia ceded 'the district of Firuza and the adjacent lands between Baba Durmaz and Lutfabad' and received Hissar and a strip near Abbasabad. The Persian claim before 1881 is covered by the Akhal region record (nominal suzerainty over the Tekke/Atek lands), so no gap is shown.
Moscow Treaty Art. 3 provided for return to Iran (never carried out); Iran dropped the claim in the 2 Dec 1954 frontier settlement.
Nominal Persian claim to the Tekke/Atek Turkmen; ended by the Akhal-Khorasan Convention, which fixed the Kopet Dag/Atrek line and ended Iran's claims beyond the Tejen.

Qajar claim to Merv asserted in expeditions (1832, 1837, 1860); the 1860 Merv disaster began 'the end of Iran's claims'; 1881 convention 'effectively ended Iran's historical claims to... Marv'. Claim was nominal.
Sarakhs was regarded as indisputably Persian; Russians took the north bank 1884-85; the frontier east of Babadurmaz was fixed in the 1893 convention.

Tehran asserted overlordship over the Baban emirs when they sought Persian backing (Fath-Ali Shah restored Abdurrahman Pasha in 1806; Persian forces took Shahrizor/Sulaymaniyah in 1822). Renounced in the Second Treaty of Erzurum ('all claim to the town and province of As Sulaymaniyah').
Persia claimed the whole Zohab province; the Second Erzurum Treaty (Art. 2) gave the western lowlands to the Ottomans and the eastern mountains plus Kirind valley to Persia.

Inferred: Persia held and claimed this lowland strip despite the 1847 cession of the Zohab lowlands, since the 1913 Protocol obliged it to evacuate it and assigned it to the Ottomans. Persia later disputed the Protocol's validity (League of Nations 1934) until the 1937 treaty reaffirmed it. Iranica ('Boundaries i. With the Ottoman Empire'): 'the areas of Naft-khana and the zone immediately to the north, around Qasr-e Shirin... together with the oil rights of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, were transferred to the Ottoman authorities' on 18 Jomada II 1332 = 15 May 1914; the 1913 Protocol line there runs 'as far as the Naft-Su... leaving Naft-Mukataasy to Turkey', then along the Naft-Deressi to the Qasr-i-Shirin road and the Jebel Hamrin chain. Extent still unsourced; rectangle kept.

Kotur dispute opened in the 1849-52 commission; Berlin 1878 Art. LX had Turkey cede 'Khotour' to Persia; Sary Kamish protocol (1880) assigned villages; the 1932 Tehran agreement gave Turkey 90 sq mi near Kotur.

Eastern flank of the Ararat massif was Persian under the Erivan/Maku frontier; ceded to Turkey after the Ararat rebellion, Tehran agreement of 23 Jan 1932. No source consulted links Bazargan (only the border crossing) to the 1932 exchange.

Iran abrogated the 1937 treaty and claimed the thalweg along the whole river; the Algiers Accord (6 Mar 1975) and the Baghdad treaty (13 June 1975) conceded it. Iraq abrogated it on 17 Sept 1980 and re-accepted it in Aug 1990; Tehran has never wavered. From 1914 to 1969 Tehran accepted the low-water line on the Iranian bank except at Muhammarah/Abadan (it contested the 1847/1913 regime before the League in 1934).

Persian jurisdiction over the Muhammarah anchorage recognised by the Second Erzurum Treaty and confirmed in the 1913 Protocol (the river itself stayed Ottoman); boundary at the thalweg here from 1914.
Tehran treaty of 4 July 1937 shifted the line to the thalweg off Abadan (Iran's main grievance: jetties in Iraqi waters).

Qajars regarded Herat as a dependency of Khorasan; Treaty of Paris (4 March 1857, ratified 2 May at Baghdad) made Persia renounce 'all claims to sovereignty over the territory and the city of Herat or the countries of Afghanistan' and any coinage, khutba or tribute. Iranica has Fath-Ali Shah establishing suzerainty c.1801 and re-imposing it in 1807 and 1814, Wikipedia calls Herat 'effectively independent' from 1801; the 1800 baseline is the Qajar claim to Khorasan's dependencies.

Nominal: the Kandahar sardars (Kohandil Khan) accepted Persian suzerainty by a treaty in the Herat campaign, and by 1842 a treaty with the Kandahar chief is reported (India Office Military Report on Persia) to have relinquished Persian claims. Evidence thin; Treaty of Paris Art. VI covers 'the countries of Afghanistan'. The Principality of Kandahar (Barakzai Dil brothers) existed 1818-1856 as a breakaway from the Durrani state; Wikipedia 'First Herat War' lists it among the supporters of Qajar Iran in 1837-38, which is the only basis found for a Persian suzerainty claim; no treaty text was found.

cites.note: 'In 1842 a treaty was concluded between the Shah and the Chief of Kandahar, by which Persia relinquished all claim to Afghan territory'

claims.note: Tehran claimed all Sistan (Persia 'gradually reclaiming Sistan' since 1772). Goldsmid's 1872 award gave Persia Sistan proper (west of the Helmand) and Afghanistan the right bank; accepted by both in spring 1873 (neither satisfied). McMahon 1903-05 re-fixed the line after the Helmand shifted.

In 1864 (1281 AH) Tehran officially claimed the whole of Makran and Baluchistan, on the basis of Nader Shah's 1736 conquest; Persia's envoy to Kalat had disclaimed designs on Kech in 1862. Goldsmid's line (notes of 1 and 4 Sept 1871) left Kech and Panjgur to Kalat.

Presumed from the 1800 baseline as part of the general Baluchistan claim (Kuhak lies inside modern Iran); the first documented formal Tehran claim to 'all Makran and Baluchistan' is 1864 (Iranica). No Kuhak-specific claim before 1871 is documented; in the notes of 1 and 4 Sept 1871 Kohuk was recorded on the Kalat side, so the claim ends on the 4 Sept 1871 signature date.

After the 1871 line Iran claimed Kuhak (a joint commission examined the boundary in 1872 and Britain agreed the line should lie east of Kuhak) and occupied it in May 1874; the Holdich agreement of 26 March 1896 formally included Kuhak in Iran. The year of the first renewed claim (1872-74) is not documented; the original start_event pointed to the 1871 Goldsmid line, which is the renunciation, not the reclaim.

Tehran treated Bahrain as a dependency of Fars: Persian rule 1753-83 (Shaykh Nasr al-Madhkur) ended with the Al Khalifa conquest of 1783, but claims were renewed repeatedly (1820s, 1861, 1871, 1927). Firmest early document: the 1822 Bruce-Farmanfarma agreement ('always subordinate to the province of Fars'), which London repudiated. Claim from 1800 is inferred. Pre-1822 evidence (India Office summary): projects for restoring Persian authority in 1783-1800 did not materialise, but in 1799 the Utub of Bahrain, alarmed by the Imam of Muscat, offered tribute to Persia and the Persian governor of Bushire received an instalment of revenue; Muscat occupied Bahrain in 1800-01; the Utub were under Wahhabi influence 1803-11; in 1823 Fars governor Farmanfarma gave the title daryabeygi to the shaikh of Sharjah/Ras al-Khaima to enlist his help in taking Bahrain. A Tehran claim in 1800-22 is therefore real but thinly documented (low).

Majlis law of 11-12 Nov 1957 declared Bahrain the 14th province. Tehran accepted the UN finding (Guicciardi mission 29 Mar-18 Apr 1970; UNSC Res. 278 of 11 May) when the Majlis approved on 14 May 1970 (184-4; Senate unanimous 18 May).

First documented explicit Tehran claim: a Persian military report of 1888 prepared for the prime minister, which Britain neither countered nor objected to (Iranica); copies of a British War Office map showing Abu Musa, the Tunbs and Farur as Persian were presented to the Shah in July 1888. No Tehran statement about Abu Musa before 1888 was found, so the claim is dated from 1888. How the Gulf island claims are dated: where the island was held by another polity (here the Qasimi shaykhs of Sharjah under British protection) the claim is dated from the first documented Tehran assertion (Abu Musa 1888, Tunbs 1903-04); where it was a dependency administered by Persian-appointed deputies (Sirri) the claim is presumed from 1800. The earliest Persian jurisdictional act is the 1788-89 arbitration by the Persian governor of Jahangira over Greater Farur, Sirri and Abu Musa; Iran's present position (islands always Iranian, administered through the Lengeh Qasimi until 1887) rests on it, but Iranica stresses that the Persian and Sharjah claims 'hinge on the interpretation' of a Qasimi confederacy that straddled both shores in 1747-1887 and the British treated Abu Musa as Sharjah's. That retrospective claim is not mapped for 1800-1887. Flag-raising incidents 1903-04. Sharjah/UAE disputes the Iranian position.

Start = first documented Tehran-side action: July 1903 the British Resident had the shaikh of Sharjah plant his flag on Greater Tonb to pre-empt a Persian move; in March 1904 a Persian customs contingent landed, removed the Sharjah flags and raised the Persian standard, and on 14 June 1904 Persia withdrew 'subject to the reservations' (status quo). Iranica also reports that the Qasimi governors of Lengeh controlled the Tonbs c.1789-1887 and that in 1864, 1873, 1879 and 1881 the Residency was seized with the ownership question, the British refusing to endorse the claims of the Qasimi of the lower Gulf; no Tehran statement about the Tunbs before 1903 was found, so the retrospective Iranian claim is not mapped for 1800-1903 (see Abu Musa for the rule). Sharjah/RAK/UAE dispute the Iranian position.
As Greater Tunb (the Lesser Tunb is treated together with it in the Persian and British sources of 1903-04).

Presumed from the 1800 baseline; NOT a documented Tehran statement. Sirri was a dependency of the Lengeh deputy governorship, held for the Persian government by Qasimi shaykhs (c.1789-1887); the Persian governor of the Jahangira district had arbitrated between the Qasimi of Lengeh and the Marazeq of Lar over Greater Farur, Sirri and Abu Musa in 1788-89. Tehran's first explicit act is 1887: in Feb 1887 the ports of Bushehr, Lengeh and Bandar Abbas with their dependent districts and islands were reorganised as 'Persian Gulf Ports'; in Sept 1887 the Qasimi governorship was dissolved and four days later a Persian garrison of 30 men, two cannon and a flagstaff landed on Sirri; Britain decided in Aug 1888 tacitly to acquiesce. The 1887 act enforced an existing claim rather than creating one, so no gap is shown (contrast Abu Musa and the Tunbs, where the claim is dated from the first documented Tehran assertion). No Tehran statement about Sirri before 1887 was found.

Tehran treated the Ka'b/Muhaysin sheikhs (Muhammarah emerged as an autonomous emirate c.1812) as its vassals in Arabistan; the Ottoman governors of Baghdad/Basra claimed the port, and the Ottoman sack of 1837 led to the Erzurum conference.

Second Erzurum (31 May 1847): Muhammarah (Khorramshahr), Khizr (Abadan) island, the anchorage and the east bank recognised as Persian (the Shatt itself stayed Ottoman); the 1913 Protocol confirmed Persian jurisdiction over the port and anchorage of Muhammarah.

Persia claimed Chabahar on the basis of Nader Shah's 1736 conquest and never renounced the claim; the first documented formal claim to all Makran and Baluchistan is 1864 (1281 AH) and Persian forces occupied the bay on 21 Feb 1872. A Chabahar-specific Tehran statement before 1864 was not found; the claim is presumed from the 1800 baseline because the parcel lies inside modern Iran.

Mirjaveh lies in Persian Sarhad and Tehran never renounced it; Britain's levy post at Kila Safaid/Padaha (1896-1905) produced a dispute that ended when the UK withdrew its claim on 13 May 1905. Claim presumed from the 1800 baseline (inside modern Iran).

control.note: British-Indian Army of the Indus with Shah Shuja from 25 April 1839; Kohan Dil Khan and his brothers went into exile in Kerman (Persia) and returned in 1842 to re-establish the principality.

control.controller_note: Sultanate of Muscat/Oman (appanage from 1792; brief interval 1804)
control.note: Persia never renounced its claim (based on Nader Shah's 1736 conquest); Persian forces under Ebrahim Khan occupied Chabahar 21 Feb 1872.

Al Khalifa shaykhs (independent from 1783; British protection from the 1820 treaty, 1861 and 1892 agreements; British-administered foreign relations)
control.note: Not a military occupation; labelled per the project convention for claimed lands ruled by a non-Iranian state. Omani occupation 1800-01 ignored.

control.controller_note: Qasimi shaykhs of Sharjah (Trucial State under British protection)
control.note: Qasimi shaykhs of Sharjah administered the island (Britain treated it as Sharjah's); not recorded before 1888 because no Tehran claim is mapped before then.

control.controller_note: Shared administration under the 29 Nov 1971 Iran-Sharjah MoU (Iranian troops in the northern sector, Sharjah police and residents elsewhere)
control.note: Status choice: 'contested' (neither side clearly held it) is retained for the shared administration. 'indirect' would mean a local ruler governing under the shah's acknowledged suzerainty, which the 1971 Iran-Sharjah MoU expressly avoided (each side kept its sovereignty claim; Iranian troops in an agreed northern sector, Sharjah police and residents elsewhere, revenue sharing); 'direct' would overstate Iranian control before 1992; 'foreign_occupation' would ignore the Iranian garrison. It is drawn as a fuzzy area, not as a war front. The MoU is dated 29 or 30 Nov 1971 in different sources; Iranian forces landed on 30 Nov.

control.controller_note: Iran
control.note: Iran expelled the foreign workers running the UAE-sponsored school, clinic and power station in April 1992 and refused entry to over 100 Sharjah teachers on 24 Aug 1992; some accounts date the end of shared administration to April 1992, the 24 Aug date is kept as the clearest break.

control.controller_note: Qasimi shaykhs (Sharjah 1904-21, Ras al-Khaimah 1921-71) under British protection
Iran (landing 29/30 Nov 1971 after armed resistance)
control.note: Some sources date the Tunb landing to the evening of 29 Nov.

control.controller_note: Qasimi shaykhs (Sharjah, then Ras al-Khaimah) under British protection
Iran
Qasimi deputy-governors of Lengeh (Persian officials)
control.note: The Qasimi deputy governors of Lengeh (Persian officials, hereditary) administered Sirri as a Lengeh dependency until their governorship was dissolved in Sept 1887.

control.controller_note: Iran
control.note: Persian garrison landed four days after the dissolution of the Qasimi governorship of Lengeh (Sept 1887); Britain acquiesced tacitly in Aug 1888.

control.controller_note: Ottoman Baghdad (Ali Rida Pasha sacked Muhammarah in 1837) vs Persia and the Muhaysin sheikhs
control.note: Ottoman governor Ali Rida Pasha sacked Muhammarah in 1837; the town was 'alternately claimed and occupied' until the Second Treaty of Erzurum gave Persia Muhammarah, Khizr island, the anchorage and the east bank.

control.controller_note: Iran (baseline record)
control.note: Baseline control. The semi-autonomous Muhaysin/Khaz'al sheikhdom (to Dec 1924), the 1857 British occupation and the 1980-82 Iraqi occupation have their own records, drawn over this one.

control.controller_note: Baluch chiefs of Sarhad (baseline record)
control.note: Baseline control. The Sarhad Baluch were practically independent until the Persian occupation of Bampur in 1849-50 and autonomous afterwards (Iranica); those periods have their own records, drawn over this one.

control.controller_note: Iran (baseline record)
control.note: UK withdrew its claim to Mirjaveh on 13 May 1905. Baseline only: Baluch-chief autonomy and the British Sarhad levy/occupation (1916-24) have their own records.

control.controller_note: Imperial Russia (Caspian naval station; Soviet Russia to 1921)
control.note: Following a Persian request for ships against Turkmen raiders (Iranica: 1254/1838), Russia built barracks and stationed warships on Ashurada; Iranica ('Gorgan vii') places the occupation in Mohammad Shah's reign (1834-48). Wikipedia gives 1837 and Qajar-era sources 1841; the earlier 1842 start was too late. Russians recognised Iranian sovereignty but refused to evacuate and returned the islands under the Persian-Soviet treaty of Feb 1921 (Iranica dates this to 13 Feb 1921; the treaty was signed 26 Feb 1921).

control.controller_note: Soviet Russia (Caspian naval station held after the revolution)
control.note: Following a Persian request for ships against Turkmen raiders (Iranica: 1254/1838), Russia built barracks and stationed warships on Ashurada; Iranica ('Gorgan vii') places the occupation in Mohammad Shah's reign (1834-48). Wikipedia gives 1837 and Qajar-era sources 1841; the earlier 1842 start was too late. Russians recognised Iranian sovereignty but refused to evacuate and returned the islands under the Persian-Soviet treaty of Feb 1921 (Iranica dates this to 13 Feb 1921; the treaty was signed 26 Feb 1921).

control.controller_note: Sheikh Mohammad Khiabani and the Democratic Party of Azerbaijan ("Azadistan")
control.note: Khiabani's armed supporters took Tabriz on 7 April 1920 (Swedish-officered police left; bazaar closed 9 April) and proclaimed Azadistan as a model of free government against the 1919 Anglo-Persian Agreement; he considered himself an Iranian nationalist, not a separatist. Cossack forces entered Tabriz on 14 Sept 1920 and Khiabani was killed. Only Tabriz's control is firmly documented. Persian-language sources used by Wikipedia ('Mohammad Khiabani's uprising') date the start to 5 April 1920; Iranica has 7 April.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

control.controller_note: Bakhtiari ilkhani/ilbegi families (Chahar Lang supremacy to 1841; Haft Lang ilkhanis from Hosein Qoli Khan, 1867; Sardar As'ad, Samsam al-Saltaneh)
control.note: Bakhtiari khans were the semi-autonomous overlords of Chahar Mahal and the Khuzestan piedmont and, in 1909, helped depose Mohammad Ali Shah and thereafter held ministries and governorates. Reza Shah detribalised them: ilkhani/ilbegi titles abolished 1933, khans arrested and some executed in 1934, territory divided 1936. The 1929-31 Bakhtiari revolt (9 July 1931 in Isfahan province) did not hold territory for a month.

control.controller_note: Baluch sardars of Bampur, Dizzak, Sarbaz, Geh and Qasr-e Qand (with Kalat and Muscat influence)
control.note: Iranica: the province was "practically independent" until Persian troops occupied Bampur in 1849.

control.controller_note: Persian governor at Bampur (Sartip Ebrahim Khan) with local rulers paying taxes; later the Barakzai (Baranzai) chiefs Mir Bahram Khan (d. 1921) and Dost Mohammad Khan (1921-28)
control.note: Bampur was garrisoned permanently from 1850; Kerman's governor campaigned against Baluch tribes in 1862. Persian influence waned after 1905; Dost Mohammad, recognised as governor of Bampur in 1921, claimed autonomy until Gen. Jahanbani's 1928 campaign; he later escaped from Tehran and was hanged on 16 Jan 1930. End month is an estimate. After the 1928-29 campaign the Iranian state continued to govern Persian Baluchistan through Iranian-appointed local sardars (Jan-Mohammad Buledi at Qasr-e Qand, Mehrab Khan Bozorgzadeh at Jaleq, Mohammadshah Mir-Moradzay at Sib, Shahbaz Khan Bozorgzadeh at Dizzak - Wikipedia 'Dost Mohammad Khan Baloch'); that quasi-indirect phase is not mapped because no end date is established, so the map shows direct control after 1928.

control.controller_note: Baluch tribes of Sarhad (Rigi, Ismailzai, Damani, Baranzai) under their sardars
control.note: Iranica: Persian Baluchistan was 'practically independent' until Persian troops occupied Bampur in 1849/50; Sarhad lay beyond even that. Frontier demarcated 1895-96.

control.controller_note: British India (Seistan Force detachments, then Sarhad Levy Corps with a garrison at Khash)
control.note: British troops were stationed at Khash from May 1916 and organised tribal levies; after the 1920 Sistan withdrawal they stayed. The "official ceremony ending the British occupation of Iranian Baluchistan" was held on 1 March 1924, when the Union Jack at Khash was replaced by the Iranian tricolour.

cites.note: cross-check; formation July 1915, Seistan Force from March 1916, last elements out Nov 1920

control.controller_note: Iranian military command (Salar Amjad) paying subsidies to Baluch chiefs; Dost Mohammad Khan claiming autonomy
control.note: Tehran took over the subsidy-and-levy arrangement; control rested on chiefs such as the Rigi chief Idu Khan. Campaigns against Dost Mohammad culminated in 1928.

control.controller_note: Britain (Bombay Marine/Government of India station; sepoy detachment)
control.note: After the General Treaty of Peace (1820) Basidu became the main British operational base in the Gulf (until about 1863); a sepoy detachment stayed to 1879, after which only a coal depot under a native agent remained until the depot moved to Henjam in 1911-12. Persian protests and claims over Qeshm never lapsed.

control.controller_note: Hereditary Khans of Bastak (Sheikh Mohammad Khan Bastaki in the 18th century; later Mohammad-Reza Khan and his father, titled Sowlat al-Molk)
control.note: The Khans of Bastak governed the district and, as late as 1854, controlled Lengeh's Qasimi sheikh (revenue collector under the governor of Bastak); a Fars governor's force from Lar captured Bastak in 1809. From 1856 the governorship of Lengeh itself went to outsiders and in 1887 Persia ended the Qasimi governorship, but that does NOT end the Bastak khans: Persian Gulf Residency monthly reports of 1912-20 (file 2297/1919) still show the Khan of Bastak (Mohammad-Reza Khan) and his father contending for the Lengeh administration, so their rule outlasted 1887. The end date of 1925 is an estimate tied to Reza Khan's consolidation in the south; the real date is unknown.

cites.note: Sheikh of Lengeh as revenue collector under the governor of Bastak, to at least 1854; cross-check

control.controller_note: Shadlu Kurdish ilkhanis (Ebrahim Khan; Najaf-Ali Khan, ilkhani from 1802; Sardar Mo'azzaz Bojnurdi in 1921)
control.note: Shadlu and other Kurdish tribes ran Bojnurd and Esfarayen; they were the force that killed Col. Pesyan in 1921. Bombing of Bojnurd on 18 May 1925 marked the collapse; forced settlement from 1929; the last Kurdish ilkhan (Faraj-Allah Khan Bicaranlu) failed to seize power in 1942. Iranica adds that in spring 1925 the Kurds of Bojnurd were 'apparently under the control of the central government' (acting against Turkmen besiegers of Bojnurd) and that from about 1925 the ilkhani system collapsed; on 16 Feb 1942 Faraj-Allah Khan Bicaranlu briefly seized Shirvan, Esfarayen, Darreh Gaz, Mane, Samalqan, Jajarm, Faruj and Quchan before being defeated (under a month; not mapped).

control.controller_note: Britain (Indian Army expeditionary force; Gen. Outram from 27 Jan 1857)
control.note: Bushehr surrendered on 9-10 Dec 1856 after the storming of Reshire (5 Dec); Borazjan was occupied 5 Feb 1857. Iranica says the British evacuated the Gulf by mid-1857; Wikipedia gives October 1857 for Bushehr.

control.controller_note: Britain (Maj. A. P. Trevor, military commander)
control.note: British forces took Bushehr on 8 Aug 1915 after the 12 July attack on the Residency, disarmed the gendarmerie and raised the Union Jack; the occupation ended by agreement on 16 Oct 1915 (Persian postal authority regained 18 Oct), and the British returned in 1916 with the SPR.

control.controller_note: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (Chabahar as a Makran/Gwadar appanage, held through Jadgal chiefs such as Din Muhammad of Dashtiari)
control.note: Lorimer: Chahbar remained an appanage of Oman until 1872. In January 1872 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of Sultan Turki, seized it; in March a Persian army expelled him (the Persian governor of Bampur, Sartip Ebrahim Khan, had asserted that Chahbar belonged to Persia). Actual Omani presence before 1872 was nominal and mediated by local chiefs.

control.controller_note: Constitutionalist forces at Rasht (Sepahdar Tonekaboni, Mo'azzed al-Saltaneh) against Mohammad Ali Shah
control.note: Rasht fell to the constitutionalists in January 1909 and became a base from which a Gilani force marched on Tehran, which fell on 13 July 1909. They rejected the shah's government rather than seeking separation. Month of the Rasht takeover is approximate.

control.controller_note: Imperial Russian garrisons at Anzali and Rasht
control.note: Russia landed troops at Anzali in April 1909 and, with Persian administration continuing, kept troops in Gilan until its evacuation in Jan-Mar 1918. The date of first occupation of Rasht itself is not fixed.

control.controller_note: Jangalis (Mirza Kuchek Khan) vs. Russian, British (Dunsterforce, Norperforce) and Qajar forces
control.note: Kuchek Khan took to the forests in October 1915; after the Russian Revolution the Jangalis ran much of Gilan's administration (1917), signed an agreement with Dunsterforce (Aug 1918, Manjil battle), were dispersed by a British-Qajar offensive in March 1919 and regrouped by summer. Russian garrisons left in early 1918; British posts (Anzali) until May 1920.

control.controller_note: Jangalis (Mirza Kuchek Khan) vs. Russian, British (Dunsterforce, Norperforce) and Qajar forces
control.note: Kuchek Khan took to the forests in October 1915; after the Russian Revolution the Jangalis ran much of Gilan's administration (1917), signed an agreement with Dunsterforce (Aug 1918, Manjil battle), were dispersed by a British-Qajar offensive in March 1919 and regrouped by summer. Russian garrisons left in early 1918; British posts (Anzali) until May 1920.

control.controller_note: Persian Socialist Soviet Republic (Kuchek Khan, Ehsanollah Khan, Haydar Khan Amu-oghlu) under Red Army protection
control.note: The Red Army landed at Anzali on 18 May 1920; the Soviet Republic of Gilan was proclaimed at Rasht on 4-6 June. After the Feb 1921 Persian-Soviet treaty the Red Army left on 8 Sept 1921 and Reza Khan's forces took Rasht in October; Kuchek died in December 1921.

control.controller_note: Imperial Russia (Baratov column)
control.note: Baratov took Hamadan in December 1915 (sources: 3 or 15 Dec). The Russians evacuated it on 9 Aug 1916 (last troops marched out that afternoon) and the Ottoman XIII Corps entered on 10 Aug 1916 (Segal 2023, citing A.C. Edwards, an eyewitness).

control.controller_note: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan)
control.note: Ottoman XIII Corps entered Hamadan on 10 Aug 1916 while Baratov's Russians held the Sultan Bulagh pass about 75 miles from Qazvin. The Ottoman advance halted at the end of its supply line; the sources consulted (Wikipedia 'Persian campaign (World War I)', citing Caven) have Baratov moving on Hamadan again in December 1916, and Hamadan changed hands that month. The end month is the least certain part (some accounts keep the Ottomans there into early 1917).

Ottoman entry 10 Aug 1916; Russian line at Sultan Bulagh

control.controller_note: Imperial Russia (Baratov corps, disintegrating)
control.note: Russian garrisons (Baratov's Caucasian Cavalry Corps) re-entered Hamadan in December 1916 and held it until the army dissolved in winter 1917-18. Start moved from 1917-03 to 1916-12 (see the Ottoman record above); low confidence.

control.controller_note: British (Dunsterforce, then Norperforce lines)
control.note: Dunsterville's advance party reached Hamadan in Feb 1918; the British kept Hamadan as a base on the Kermanshah-Qazvin line until Norperforce left on 21 April 1921.

control.controller_note: Britain (Royal Navy/Government of India coaling depot and naval base)
control.note: A telegraph station had been tolerated since the late 1860s; the coaling depot moved from Basidu to Henjam in 1911/12 and by 1913 it was the main British naval base. Persia had granted only a telegraph concession; Reza Shah demanded evacuation and the British abandoned the station in 1935.

control.controller_note: Iran (defenders) vs. Iraq (besiegers)
control.note: Iraqi forces encircled Abadan from late 1980 but never took the city; the siege was lifted on 27 Sept 1981 (Operation Samen-ol-A'emeh). Start date is the invasion date; full encirclement came later.

control.controller_note: Iraq
control.note: Iraq entered Dehloran, Qasr-e Shirin, Sumar, Naft Shahr, Sar-e Pol-e Zahab and Mousiyan on 12 July 1988 and withdrew from the towns after Iran accepted the ceasefire; but reports in August 1990 say Iraq still held about 2,600 km2 (1,000 sq mi) of Iranian territory, which it began to evacuate on 16-17 Aug 1990 (a UN report of 24 Sept 1990 said withdrawal was almost complete). Locations of the pockets were not identified in sources found. UNIIMOG's own background says that by end-September 1990 withdrawal to the international boundaries was 'almost complete' with a few locations where forces of each side were still on the wrong side, and that by end-January 1991 Iraq had withdrawn from 23 of 29 disputed positions (Iran from 13 of 17). The pockets were therefore a handful of border positions, not a large contiguous area, and the Aug 1990 '2,600 km2' figure comes from press reports of Saddam Hussein's offer. Record kept at low confidence.

cites.note: cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988

control.controller_note: Iraq
control.note: The Iraqi attack on Khorramshahr began on 22 Sept 1980; the city fell on 24 Oct (Iraqi control effectively complete 10 Nov) after a 34-day battle and was liberated on 24 May 1982 in Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas. Iraq announced its withdrawal from remaining Iranian territory on 20 June 1982.

control.controller_note: Iraq vs. Iran (Mehran changed hands several times)
control.note: Iraq captured Mehran in the 1980 invasion; Wikipedia ('Battle of Mehran (1986)') calls the May 1986 capture the third time Iraq took it, so Iraqi control before 1986 was not continuous, and the Mehran article says the Iraqis had been driven out by 1982-83. Dates of the first recapture are not established, so the whole span is shown as contested (low confidence).

control.controller_note: Iraq (II Corps)
control.note: Iraq recaptured Mehran on 15-19 May 1986 ("for the third time"); Iran retook the area in Operation Karbala-1 (30 June-3 July 1986) and defeated a Republican Guard counter-attack on 4 July.

control.controller_note: Iraqi forces with the Mojahedin-e Khalq (Operation Forty Stars)
control.note: On 18 June 1988 Iraq and the MEK crushed two Iranian divisions and seized Mehran; Iraqi regulars left after three days and the MEK stayed. Wikipedia says Iran retook Mehran in Operation Mersad (26 July); the end date is uncertain.

control.controller_note: Iraq
control.note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of the Dasht-e Azadegan plain (the Susangerd salient). Iran relieved a siege of Susangerd in Nov 1980 and recaptured Bostan and 70 villages on 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981 (Operation Tariq al-Quds); the rest was cleared by June 1982. Holdings varied by month. Iranica ('Iraq vii'): after Fath ol-Mobin (22 March 1982, Shush-Dezful) and the 22 March offensive north of Bostan, the stage of 24 April-12 May 1982 'drove the Iraqi troops back to Khorramshahr from the Ahvaz-Susangird area'; the end is therefore May 1982 rather than Iraq's general withdrawal announcement in June. Khorramshahr itself (separate record) fell on 24-25 May.

control.controller_note: Iraq
control.note: Iraq took Qasr-e Shirin on the first days of the invasion and advanced on the Kermanshah and Ilam fronts (Sar-e Pol-e Zahab, Gilan-e Gharb, Musian/Dehloran); the central-front lines were pushed back in Dec 1981-Jan 1982 and Iraq announced its withdrawal on 20 June 1982. Town-by-town dates are not established here.

cites.note: cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988

control.controller_note: Bakhtiari constitutionalist khans (Samsam al-Saltaneh, Sardar As'ad)
control.note: Bakhtiari forces took Isfahan in early 1909 and, with Sardar As'ad (who entered the city on 14 May 1909 per Iranica), marched on Tehran with the Gilan force, which fell on 13 July 1909. Dates are approximate.

control.controller_note: Kalhor chiefs (Davud Khan, killed 1912 fighting for Salar al-Dowleh; his successor Abbas Khan), with Guran and Sanjabi subordinate
control.note: Iranica: Davud Khan Kalhor, who 'ruled the tribe in the early 1900s', started as a peddler and made himself 'the absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border', also subjugating the Guran and Sanjabi; he held the Qajar title Sardar-e Mozaffar and governed the Kalhor district. He was killed fighting for Salar al-Dowleh (1911 per British records and Wikipedia; 1912 per Iranica) and his successor Abbas Khan was imprisoned by Reza Shah in 1926. Before c.1900 the Kalhor were one of several tribes inside the province of Kermanshah, governed from the city by Qajar princes (Kalhor and Zangana levies served those governors, e.g. against the Bakhtiari in 1830), with no autonomous Kalhor ruler; those years are left as direct. The exact start of Davud Khan's ascendancy (c.1900) is approximate.

cites.note: cross-check; Qajar-era role of the Kalhor and Zangana under the governors of Kermanshah

control.controller_note: Salar al-Dowleh (Abolfath Mirza) with Kalhor, Jaf, Sanjabi and Lur followers vs. Bakhtiari/government forces
control.note: Mohammad Ali Shah's brother occupied Sanandaj by 17 July 1911, seized Kermanshah (given up to plunder) and, per Wikipedia, Hamadan; he marched on Tehran, won a first battle near Malayer and was decisively beaten near Saveh by Amir Mofakham Bakhtiari (his Kalhor ally Davud Khan died in this campaign: 1911 per the British records and Wikipedia, 1912 per Iranica). The revolt did not end there: he remained in the Kermanshah-Kurdistan area until Farman Farma's 1912 expedition (Persian Gulf Administration Report 1911-14: 'In July Salar-ed-Dowleh fled from Kermanshah, on the arrival of Farman Farma... and left for Luristan and Kurdistan'), so the end is moved from Dec 1911 to July 1912. Control of each town in between is not established; status stays contested.

control.controller_note: Committee for the Defence of Iran's Independence / National (Provisional) Government of Kermanshah under Nezam al-Saltaneh Mafi, backed by German and Ottoman agents
control.note: Nationalists left Tehran for Qom (Nov 1915) and set up an anti-Allied government at Kermanshah; Ottoman and German forces occupied the city in 1915-16. The government fell back before the Russian entry on 26 Feb 1916.

control.controller_note: Imperial Russian Caucasian Cavalry Corps (Gen. Baratov)
control.note: Russian forces broke through at Sahneh (22 Feb), took Bisotun (24 Feb) and entered Kermanshah on 26 Feb 1916; the Ottoman XIII Corps (Ali Ihsan) retook it on 2 July 1916.

cites.note: cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916
cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

control.controller_note: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan) and German officers, with the returned Persian nationalist government
control.note: The Ottomans held Kermanshah from 2 July 1916 until their retreat after the fall of Baghdad (11 March 1917); the exact evacuation date is not established. Wikipedia ('Battle of Khanaqin') says the Russians occupied Khanaqin after Ali Ihsan was recalled to Baghdad in Feb 1917, so the Ottoman hold on Kermanshah ended between Feb and mid-March 1917; the exact date remains unknown.

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations
cross-check; Ali Ihsan recalled Feb 1917, Russians occupy Khanaqin

control.controller_note: Imperial Russia (Baratov's remaining troops, disintegrating after the revolution)
control.note: After the Ottoman retreat Russian forces re-entered the Kermanshah area; most Russian troops left Persia between December 1917 and March 1918, a few under Baratov passing into British service. Dates low-confidence.

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

control.controller_note: British (Dunsterforce lines of communication, then Norperforce)
control.note: The British held the Mesopotamia-Kermanshah-Hamadan-Qazvin-Anzali road line; Dunsterville reached Hamadan in Feb 1918. The garrisons were progressively reduced; Norperforce withdrew on 21 April 1921. Persian civil authority continued.

control.controller_note: Britain (East India Company/Bombay Marine; Residency moved from Bushehr to Kharg)
control.note: Occupied on 19 June 1838 in response to Mohammad Shah's siege of Herat; the Persians lifted the siege on 9 Sept 1838 but, "owing to the shifty character of their subsequent diplomacy", the island was not evacuated until March 1842.

control.controller_note: Britain (naval force; island garrisoned through the Anglo-Persian War)
control.note: Occupied 4 Dec 1856; Iranica: held until spring 1858 although the main forces left in 1857.

control.controller_note: Ka'b sheikhs of Fallahiyeh, then Khaz'al (decrees of 1903 granting Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla and Mashur as perpetual holdings)
control.note: The Ka'b heartland and the coastal lands behind Mohammerah were held by Arab sheikhs acknowledging the shah. Pre-1897 holdings and rulers are only loosely characterised here.

control.controller_note: Sheikh Khaz'al (administrator of northern Khuzestan from 1907)
control.note: Sardar Mokarram (later Nezam al-Saltaneh) placed Khaz'al in charge of northern Khuzestan in 1907; by 1911 the governorship "does not confer any great powers, most of the country being under the rule of the Shaikh" with only Dezful and Shushtar outside his control.

control.controller_note: Khans of Boir Ahmad (Garmsir/Sardsir), the Noi and other Kuhgiluya khans; Mamasani chief Emamqoli Khan
control.note: The tribal khans fell foul of the Qajars (Mohammad-Taher Khan blinded c.1800) but generally ruled their districts under nominal Qajar suzerainty with the Fars governor's backing at times. Tang-e Tamradi (Aug 1930) was a major tribal defeat of Reza Shah's army.

control.controller_note: Boir Ahmad / Kohgiluyeh / Mamasani khans vs. Reza Shah's army
control.note: After the Tamradi defeat (heavy losses - Iranica Boir Ahmadi: "said to have exceeded 1,000 casualties"; Fars iv gives about 400 killed; Aug 1930) the khans eventually surrendered and were executed in 1932; a military government then imposed order for the next decade.

control.controller_note: Boir Ahmad and Kohgiluyeh khans (tribal political system "rebounded with amazing vigor")
control.note: After Reza Shah's abdication central authority collapsed locally and tribal politics revived. In 1962-63 two khans resisted land reform, ambushed government forces at Tang-e Gochestan/Gachina Pass and were crushed in June 1963; thereafter the area was under tight security-force control.

control.controller_note: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic
control.note: Kurdish forces took the towns and garrisons of Paveh and Marivan region in March 1979; the army retook Paveh in the August 1979 offensive and mountain areas remained insurgent until 1983-84.

control.controller_note: Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari (Najafi Lari), a pro-constitution mujtahid
control.note: In 1909 he proclaimed a revolt, issued his own postage stamps (in use March-May 1909) and, per Iranica, "ruled Larestan until the spring of 1915", when the governor-general of Fars sent Habib-Allah Khan Qavam al-Molk to pacify it. Lorimer-based accounts have him driven from Lar and returning in August 1909 and later deported to Shiraz; continuity of control is uncertain.

control.controller_note: Qawasim (Qasimi) sheikhs of Lengeh (Sheikh Qazib ibn Rashid last)
control.note: The Qasimi sheikh administered Lengeh for the Persian government from about 1789 as revenue collector under the governor of Bastak/Fars. In Feb 1887 Persia created the "Gulf Ports" governorate; in September 1887 the Qasimi governorship was dissolved, Sheikh Qazib was arrested and a Persian garrison landed; Sheikh Mohammad ibn Khalifa briefly seized Lengeh in 1898-99 before Ahmad Khan Daryabeigi retook it in March 1899.

control.controller_note: Pish-e Kuh Lur tribes under their own chiefs (Qajar governor-general sat at Khorramabad)
control.note: The wali dynasty of Luristan was overthrown in 1796 and replaced at Khorramabad by a governor-general, but the highland tribes kept their own organisation; the Pish-e Kuh was "largely outside control" until Reza Khan's army went in (April 1921 onward).

control.controller_note: Lur tribes vs. Reza Khan's army
control.note: The army deployed to Luristan in April 1921, took Borujerd (Oct 1923) and Khorramabad (Nov 1923), met a major revolt in May 1924 and the last major engagement in 1926. Wikipedia says direct control came in 1928; Iranica says war dragged on to 1933 but migration was banned from 1929.

control.controller_note: Mukri khans/emirs of Mukriyan as Qajar-appointed hereditary governors (Sauj Bulaq/Mahabad)
control.note: Mukriyan, south of Lake Urmia, was ruled by hereditary Mokri khans who served the Qajars as governors of Savojbolagh (Sayf al-Din Khan, d. 1891/2, held the post several times; his son Hosein Khan was killed in the Ottoman attack of 1914). Their power was eroded after Ubeydullah's 1880 invasion: the Qajar state built the Savujbulagh garrison in 1883 (Sayadi 2019: 'a manifestation of the exclusion of the Mukris from the Qajar political power structure'), so 1883 is used as the end. Not independently dated to the month; some accounts keep Mokri influence into the 1910s.

cites.note: cross-check; Sayf al-Din Khan and Hosein Khan as governors of Savojbolagh

control.controller_note: Local Kurdish chiefs and the Society for the Revival of Kurdistan (Komala-i Jiyanewey Kurdistan, 1942) under Qazi Muhammad; Soviet zone
control.note: After the Iranian army collapsed in Aug-Sept 1941 Kurdish leaders returned and rearmed; Soviet forces held the zone to the north and the Iranian gendarmerie and army were driven out of the Mahabad area. Qazi Muhammad led the Komala (1942) and the KDP (founded Sept 1945). Per British-zone accounts, southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj was under British occupation, while the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the two zones; by 1945 the Iranian government effectively controlled Kurdish areas only south of the Saqqez-Baneh-Sardasht line. Start date approximate.

control.controller_note: Republic of Mahabad (Qazi Muhammad, president)
control.note: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') has Qazi Muhammad inaugurating the Kurdish Republic at Mahabad on 15 December 1945; Wikipedia gives 22 Jan 1946 for the formal proclamation and presidency. Because the question here is when a rival administration actually replaced Tehran's, 15 Dec 1945 is used (the formal proclamation of Jan 1946 is listed as its own event). Territory: Mahabad, Bukan, Naghadeh, Piranshahr and Oshnavieh (Sardasht usually added); the republic claimed but did not hold Urmia, Khoy and Salmas. After the Soviets left (May 1946) it was isolated; Iranian troops entered Mahabad on 15-17 Dec 1946.

control.controller_note: KDPI and allied Kurdish councils at Mahabad
control.note: Mahabad stayed in Kurdish hands from early March 1979 (KDPI held the military base) until the army, using F-4s and over 100 tanks, took it on 3 Sept 1979; Sardasht, Bukan and Piranshahr fell on 4-6 Sept. Start is approximate (Feb-Mar 1979).

control.controller_note: KDPI peshmerga vs. IRGC and army
control.note: Qasemlu returned to Mahabad on 20 Oct 1979 as rebels retook the town; in Nov 1979 Kurds held most roads and rural areas. After the spring 1980 government offensive retook the cities, the KDPI controlled "a major portion of Iranian Kurdistan, excluding the towns" in 1981-82; IRGC and Iranian forces drove them out in 1982-83 and the KDPI left for Iraq by early 1984.

control.controller_note: Nader Mirza Afshar (grandson of Nader Shah), backed by the Afghan rulers of Herat
control.note: After Agha Mohammad Khan's death (1797) Nader Mirza returned to Mashhad and styled himself sovereign of Khorasan. Fath-Ali Shah failed in 1799 and 1801, besieged the city in 1802 and Mohammad-Vali Mirza took it in early 1803; Nader was blinded and executed in Tehran. Reach beyond the Mashhad district is not established.

control.controller_note: Mohammad-Hasan Khan Salar (son of Asaf al-Dowleh) with local khans and ulama
control.note: Mashhad rose on 25 Aug 1848, just before Mohammad Shah's death in early September, and held out against Hamza Mirza and then Sultan Morad Mirza; besieged from June 1849, it surrendered on 13 or 23 March 1850. Salar was executed on 29 April 1850. Iranica dates the whole revolt c.1847-51; the day-level chronology comes from Wikipedia only.

cites.note: cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology

control.controller_note: Ka'b / Muhaysin sheikhs of Mohammerah (Hajji Jabir) under Qajar suzerainty with Ottoman claims
control.note: The Ka'b and later Muhaysin sheikhs "were for two centuries the most powerful chieftains of south-western Persia". Muhammara's allegiance shifted between Persia and the Ottomans.

cites.note: cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum

control.controller_note: Ottoman Baghdad (Ali Rida Pasha) vs. Persia over the Muhaysin sheikhdom
control.note: In 1837 Ali Rida Pasha captured and destroyed Muhammara and the Ka'b paid homage to the Ottomans; the town was "alternately claimed and occupied" until the Second Treaty of Erzurum (31 May 1847), Article II, ceded Mohammerah and Khizr island to Persia. Duration of the Ottoman occupation is not established.

cites.note: cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum

control.controller_note: Muhaysin sheikhs of Mohammerah (Hajji Jabir, Sheikh Thamer, Sheikh Yusuf)
control.note: After Erzurum the sheikhs remained semi-autonomous under Persian suzerainty.
