control.controller_note: Britain (Indian Army expeditionary force, Gen. Outram)
control.note: Mohammerah fell on 26-27 March 1857 after naval bombardment; the flotilla reached Ahvaz on 1 April; hostilities ceased about 4 April and the Treaty of Paris was ratified on 2 May. British forces left in mid-1857 (the main force sailed for India in May-June because of the Mutiny); exact evacuation date not established.

control.controller_note: Muhaysin sheikhs; Sheikh Khaz'al Khan (sheikh from June 1897)
control.note: Khaz'al succeeded his assassinated brother Mazal in June 1897, was recognised as Sardar Arfa' (1902), enjoyed British protection (assurances 1899-1908; KCIE 1910/1917) and ruled a "semi-independent realm". On 6 Dec 1924 he submitted to Reza Khan at Ahvaz; he was seized on 18 April 1925 and held in Tehran until his death (27 May 1936). The 1857-97 part of this span is only loosely characterised.

control.controller_note: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (Al Bu Sa'id) under lease from the Qajar shahs
control.note: Under a Persian firman of 1793/94 the Sultan administered Bandar Abbas, the Minab-Khamir coastal strip and the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz for 75 years (garrison of 120 Nubians and 80 Arabs in 1811). Mulla Hosein of Qeshm seized Bandar Abbas after 1804; the Qasimi and the Bombay Marine contested Qeshm c.1806-10. A 1855 accord limited the lease to 20 years at 16,000 tomans a year; the Qajars regained the port in October 1868 amid dynastic trouble in Muscat.

control.controller_note: Ottoman Empire (troops on the orders of the vali of Baghdad, with Sunni Kurdish tribes)
control.note: The Ottomans began occupying Persian frontier districts on 23 May 1906 (Behik in Baradost), taking Dasht, Mergever and parts of Sardasht, Bana, Ganjachin and Baradost; Mergever was occupied again on 3 Aug 1907. Pressure by Russia and Britain pushed them back around 1911-12; the withdrawal was incomplete and intermittent. End date is approximate.

control.controller_note: Col. Mohammad-Taqi Khan Pesyan, commander of the Khorasan Gendarmerie, at Mashhad
control.note: Pesyan was made military governor-general by the post-coup government on 2-3 April 1921. After Qavam al-Saltaneh became premier (late May) and sent Najd al-Saltaneh as governor, Pesyan resumed full control in July and defied Tehran until killed fighting Kurdish forces under Sardar Mo'azzaz Bojnurdi at Quchan on 3 Oct 1921. Wikipedia counts the 'Autonomous Government of Khorasan' from 2 April; the rebel phase is dated here from c. June-July.

control.controller_note: Valis of Pusht-e Kuh (hereditary Faili Lur 'Vali dynasty': Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara to c.1900-01, then his son Gholam-Reza Khan, titled Sarim al-Saltaneh/Sardar Ashrafi)
control.note: After 1796 the wali family withdrew from Khorramabad to Pusht-e Kuh, where 'quasi-autonomous governors (wali)' ruled until about 1929 (Iranica). Wali names confirmed: Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara, succeeded around 1900-01 by his son Gholam-Reza Khan, who 'only tacitly acknowledged his vassal status to the Qajars with annual tribute' (hence indirect), held the rank of major-general and fled to Baghdad with his valuables in 1928-29 rather than accept Reza Shah's invitation to Tehran; he died in Baghdad in 1939. An account of the vali fleeing to Iraq with Simko in 1922 is contradicted by this chronology.

cites.note: cross-check; citing Afshar Sistani 1993 and Amanolahi 2002

control.controller_note: Khozeimeh 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan Heshmat al-Molk; Amir Esma'il Shawkat al-Molk, to 1904; Amir Mohammad Ebrahim Shawkat al-Molk, governor 1904-1924, then his two nephews, incl. Amir Ma'soum Khan, 'the last ruling amir')
control.note: Hereditary local rulers of Birjand/Qa'en acknowledged the Qajars and acted as their governors (Iranica: 'in practice the administration of large parts of [Khorasan] was in the hands of local tribal khans', among them the Khozeima 'Alam of Birjand and the Qa'enat). Shawkat al-Molk was governor 1904-1924; he resigned in 1924 handing power to two nephews and moved to Tehran, was governor of Fars 1937 and returned to Birjand in 1942 (d. 1944). The family's hereditary hold ended sometime in the 1930s; no source gives a date, so 1935 is a marker only. Mirza Rafi' Khan's rebellion from the citadel of Furg (1850s) was put down.

control.controller_note: Qashqai ilkhanis (Jani Khan, ilkhani from 1818/19; Mohammad-Ali Khan 1823-52; Mohammad-Qoli Khan 1852-67/8; Esmail Khan Soulat al-Dowleh from 1904)
control.note: The Qashqai ilkhanate controlled Fars' grazing lands and routes, bowing to the shah at times (Mohammad-Ali Khan was held at court in 1836) and dominating Fars during the weak central rule of 1909-21 (1911 civil war with the Qavami; anti-British rising in 1918; Soulat al-Dowleh reinstated as ilkhani by Mosaddeq in late 1920). This phase ends in 1926: Iranica says that in 1926 Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were summoned to Tehran as deputies and became virtual prisoners, and 'military governors were assigned to the various Qashqai tribes' with conscription and a new tax system - i.e. direct rule 1926-29. Highly variable autonomy; treated as a single phase.

control.controller_note: Qashqai (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan) and allied tribes vs. Reza Shah
control.note: The 1929 rising began in spring (the Khamseh Baharlu drove officials out of Darab at the end of April and took Fasa on 9 May); on 4 June the Qashqai closed the Bushehr road and then the Isfahan road, isolating Shiraz, which was under siege by mid-June; on 10 July the government flew Soulat al-Dowleh from prison to Shiraz to negotiate; the Khamseh occupied the eastern towns and the Baharlu reached the Kerman frontier; by summer the rebels held 'the whole province of Fars' outside the cities (Iranica 'Fars iv'). It ended with the August 1929 truce and amnesty. The truce withdrew the military governors; the abortive 1932 rebellion is not documented as holding territory.

cites.note: cross-check; summarising the British Persian Gulf Administration Reports 1926-38: Darab end April, Fasa 9 May, roads closed 4 June, Soulat released 10 July

control.controller_note: Qashqai under Nasser Khan (ilkhani) and Khosrow Khan, with German agent Schulze-Holthus from 1942
control.note: After Reza Shah's abdication (16 Sept 1941) the brothers escaped from Tehran, proclaimed themselves ilkhani and resumed nomadism; Persian troops were dispatched only in spring 1943 and heavy fighting followed (200+ soldiers killed at Semirom, 1943).

control.controller_note: Qashqai (Nasser Khan) under a treaty granting autonomy and arms in exchange for army garrisons
control.note: The 1943-44 agreement left the tribes armed and largely self-governing while allowing garrisons; the confederacy enjoyed "almost complete autonomy" through 1945-53.

control.controller_note: Southern tribes' "Sa'adun"/South Resistance movement vs. the Qavam government
control.note: In September 1946 Nasser Khan convened a conference of the southern tribes which rose against Qavam; the Qashqai took Kazerun and Abadeh and broke through Shiraz's outer defences until Qavam dismissed the Tudeh ministers and met demands (Oct 1946). Duration about one to one and a half months.

control.controller_note: Qashqai (Four Brothers: Nasser, Malek-Mansur, Mohammad-Hosein, Khosrow Khan)
control.note: Near-complete autonomy continued until the 1953 coup; in 1954 the brothers were exiled and their property confiscated.

control.controller_note: Qashqai insurgents (Khosrow Khan Qashqai) vs. IRGC
control.note: After an attempt to arrest Khosrow Khan in June 1980, Qashqai insurgents "defied the central government" for two years from camps in the mountains until a night attack by the Revolutionary Guards in April 1982; Khosrow Khan was executed on 8 Oct 1982. This was a mobile insurgency from mountain camps, not control of the Qashqai counties; the Revolutionary Guards held the towns and roads. Shown at low confidence: control may in fact have stayed direct.

control.controller_note: British North Persia Force (Norperforce)
control.note: Formed 16 Sept 1918 from Dunsterforce remnants with its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil and a battalion at Zanjan; about 6,000 men in 1918, 3,600 by 26 Oct 1920; completely withdrawn into Mesopotamia on 21 April 1921, leaving its arms to the Persian Cossacks. Persian administration continued.

control.controller_note: Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanis of Quchan (e.g. Reza-Qoli Khan, defeated by Abbas Mirza in 1832; Sam Khan)
control.note: Kurdish khans held the Quchan marches as hereditary governors, fielding thousands of horsemen and acknowledging the shah only intermittently. Reza Khan's bombing of Bojnurd (18 May 1925) opened the end of the Kurdish ilkhani system; end date is therefore a convenience marker, not a precise date for Quchan. Abbas Mirza razed the Quchan fortress and exiled Reza-Qoli Khan after the 1832 battle (13,000 Kurds against 19,000 men); Iranica nonetheless says the Za'faranlu kept their tribal structure and ilkhani leadership throughout the Qajar era (Sam Khan fought for the shah against Salar and at Herat), and that Chenaran and Darreh Gaz were 'from time to time' under the governor of Khorasan's direct rule. So 'indirect' is retained, with brief direct episodes.

control.controller_note: Imperial Russian army (Gen. Paskevich)
control.note: Tabriz was taken on 13 Oct 1827, Urmia on 28 Jan 1828 and Ardabil on 8 Feb 1828. Turkmenchay (22 Feb 1828) tied evacuation to indemnity instalments. Kinneir reported on 12 March 1828 that he had negotiated 'the immediate evacuation of Azerbijan, with the exception of Khoee' and that the Russians were 'duly preparing to withdraw'; Paskevich left Tabriz in March. The end is therefore set at April 1828 (low); Khoy is mapped separately.

cites.note: cross-check; Tabriz 13 Oct 1827, Urmia 28 Jan 1828, Ardabil 8 Feb 1828
Paskevich leaving Tabriz, evacuation of Khoy tied to indemnity instalments

control.controller_note: Hasan Khan Salar and his Turkmen/Kurdish/local allies
control.note: After Hamza Mirza withdrew, Salar dominated most of Khorasan; the government counter-offensive retook Sabzevar (9 March 1849) and Neyshabur (21 March 1849). Start date is approximate (late summer/autumn 1848).

cites.note: cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology

control.controller_note: Ardalan valis of Senneh (Sanandaj); last wali Amanollah Khan Ardalan
control.note: The Ardalan family ruled Kurdistan as hereditary vali under the Qajars. In 1284/1867-68 Naser al-Din Shah ended the vilayet's special status and appointed his uncle Farhad Mirza Mo'tamed al-Dowleh governor of the province of Kurdistan.

control.controller_note: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic (army, IRGC)
control.note: Kurdish groups seized garrisons in Sanandaj (17-19 March 1979), Saqqez, Marivan and Paveh; Khomeini declared jihad on 17 Aug 1979 and the government retook Sanandaj and Saqqez by early September. In 1981-82 the Kurds held most of the countryside outside the towns; IRGC pushed them out in 1982-83 and the KDPI withdrew to Iraq by early 1984 (Komala persisted slightly longer). Towns and countryside flipped repeatedly; the whole span is coded contested.

control.controller_note: Shahsevan tribal khans ("the time of the independent khans")
control.note: Russia closed the Moghan frontier to the Shahsevan in 1884 and between 1884 and 1922 the Shahsevan operated with minimal central authority. They were among the first major tribes pacified and disarmed by Reza Khan's army in winter-spring 1922-23. Status before 1884 (Qajar-appointed governors with tribal chiefs) is not recorded here. Iranica ('Shahsevan'): 'virtually independent of central government for nearly four decades'; the chiefs 'usually controlled the region... focused on the city of Ardabil and smaller urban centers' until Reza Khan's army pacified them in winter-spring 1922-23; a Russian force of 5,000 under Gen. Fidarov campaigned against them in 1912. They are shown as outside state control because Iranica describes no acknowledgment of the shah; autonomy under the shah is arguable.

control.controller_note: Ismail Agha "Simko" of the Shikak (base at Chehriq castle)
control.note: Simko established authority west of Lake Urmia in 1918-19, plundered Urmia in winter 1920, defeated government forces at Tasuj (March 1921) and was joined in summer 1921 by the Mamash, Mangur and Piran. He was defeated by Reza Khan's army in summer 1922 and fled to Iraq; he returned and rebelled again in 1926 and was killed on 30 June 1930 at Ushnu. Persian authority existed only in a few towns.

control.controller_note: Simko and the Shikak
control.note: Wikipedia (single source) places Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) in Simko's hands after the death of Maj. Malakzadeh and about 600 gendarmes in October 1921, with control extending to Sardasht and Baneh by 1922. Treat as low-confidence.

control.controller_note: Local Sistani chiefs (Sarbandi, Kayani maliks; Ali Khan Sarbandi) with Persian and Afghan claims overlapping
control.note: Sistan was disputed between Persia and Afghan rulers and run by local chiefs. Ali Khan accepted Persian allegiance in 1857, unpopularly. The Goldsmid arbitration of 1872 awarded Persian (west) Sistan to Persia; Persian governors followed from December 1873.

control.controller_note: Persian governors with the 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan, then Shawkat al-Molk)
control.note: Iranica: Mir 'Alam Khan drove insurgents out of Sistan and added it to his Qa'enat amirate under Naser al-Din Shah. Sistanis rebelled against the Qa'en chief in Dec 1872 (shut him in Nasirabad); a Persian governor (Samsam al-Mulk, then Mohammad Ja'far Khan, Dec 1873) followed.

control.controller_note: British India: East Persia Cordon (July 1915), Seistan Force (from March 1916; commander Col. J. M. Wilkeley, then R. E. H. Dyer from Feb 1916)
control.note: British-Indian troops held Sistan to bar German agents from Afghanistan; the Persian governor remained but the force dominated Nasratabad and the border. The cordon later extended north via Birjand to Mashhad and (from 1918) to the Transcaspian line. Last elements left Persia in November 1920.

cites.note: cross-check; formation July 1915, Seistan Force from March 1916, last elements out Nov 1920

control.controller_note: 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat as governors of Sistan
control.note: After the British withdrawal the Alam family governed Sistan and Qa'enat as quasi-hereditary governors: Shawkat al-Molk had full authority in 1921 and resigned in 1924 in favour of two nephews (Iranica). Weakly documented; the 1935 end is a marker only.

control.controller_note: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
control.note: Sykes landed at Bandar Abbas in March 1916 to raise the South Persia Rifles (authorised strength 11,000; about 3,300 infantry and 450 cavalry by mid-1917); the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. Persian civil governors remained. Whether this deserves the occupation label is debatable (the Qajar government assented under pressure). Kerman (from June 1916) and Shiraz (from Nov 1916) are mapped separately.

control.controller_note: Hereditary governors of Tabas (Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas' family; Zangu'i khans; Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' under Naser al-Din Shah)
control.note: Per the Gazetteer of Persia vol. I (c.1910) the Tabas governorship was hereditary: Nader Shah gave the district to 'Ali Murad Khan of the Zangu'i (Arab, related to the Khozeima amirs of Qa'en) and 'the same family still govern[s] the district'; the older Vakil-i-Tabas family also held it. Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' (d. 1894) was succeeded by his eldest son 'Ali Akbar Khan. The khan paid a fixed sum to the shah and was otherwise left to do much as he pleased. The family was still in office around 1910, so the end cannot be earlier; no source gives its end, so 1935 is an estimate tied to Pahlavi centralisation.

cites.note: Tabas governorship hereditary in the family of Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas'; also Iranica 'Khorasan xi' extract naming the Zangu'i khans of Tabas

control.controller_note: Anjoman of Tabriz and constitutionalist fighters (Sattar Khan, Baqer Khan)
control.note: Tabriz refused Mohammad Ali Shah's coup of 23 June 1908 and withstood a royalist siege for ten months until Russian troops entered on 30 April 1909. The city sought to restore the constitution, not to secede.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

control.controller_note: Imperial Russia (General Snarski's expeditionary force; later Russian garrisons in Tabriz and along the Julfa road)
control.note: Russian troops held Tabriz from 30 April 1909; after the Fedayeen attack of 21 Dec 1911 Russia re-entered after shelling on 31 Dec 1911 and executed about 1,200. Russia evacuated on 17 Dec 1914 and the Ottomans (Kurdish irregulars and regulars) held Tabriz 8-31 Jan 1915 (under a month) before Russia returned; last Russians left 28 Feb 1918. Iranian administration continued throughout.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

control.controller_note: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
control.note: Ottoman forces entered Tabriz on 8 June 1918 (Wikipedia's other date: 18 June) and left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918); exact evacuation date not established.

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations
cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

control.controller_note: Khans of Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah) under the governor of Bushehr
control.note: Tribal khans of the Bushehr hinterland controlled their districts and acknowledged the Qajars loosely. Baseline characterisation only.

control.controller_note: Tangestani/Dashti tribal forces (Rais Ali Delvari, killed 2 Sept 1915; Shaikh Hosein Khan Chahkutahi; Zair Khidr) with German agent Wassmuss vs. the British and pro-British khans
control.note: The tribes attacked the British Residency at Bushehr on 12 July 1915, fought the British after the occupation of Bushehr (8 Aug 1915) and kept the hinterland in revolt, joined by the Qashqai in 1918, until the rising subsided (influenza, British pressure). Some sources say Tangestani resistance lasted to 1921.

control.controller_note: Qara'i khans: Eshaq Khan (strangled 8 July 1816) then his son Mohammad Khan (1816-32)
control.note: Eshaq Khan Qara'i ruled Torbat-e Heydarieh as a quasi-independent magnate under Fath-Ali Shah (at times effective master of Mohammad-Vali Mirza's Khorasan). Abbas Mirza captured Mohammad Khan by trickery in 1832, ending Qara'i independence; afterwards Qajar-appointed governors ruled.

control.controller_note: Yomut and Goklen (Guklan) tribal leaders
control.note: Turkmen of the Gorgan plain raided Khorasan and Astarabad and beat Persian armies (1858 near Qarri-qal'a; 1860 at Merv). Qajar governors of Astarabad held the town and a few forts; the plain itself was outside effective Persian control. Some Goklen paid taxes or migrated under pressure.

control.controller_note: Turkmen tribal chiefs under nominal Persian governors of Astarabad (Persian posts, tax-collection, Russian border pressure)
control.note: After the Russian conquest of the Akhal Teke and the Akhal-Khorasan convention (1881) the Yomut/Goklen lost their steppe hinterland and were drawn into limited Persian tax/administrative arrangements. Reza Khan's army moved in and disarmed the Turkmen in 1925; Gonbad-e Qabus became the settlement centre. The 1881 start is a convenience marker.

control.controller_note: Turkmen People's Councils / Turkmen Cultural and Political Society vs. IRGC
control.note: After the Revolution Turkmen councils (shuras) ran local affairs; open clashes in March 1979 ended in a ceasefire on 3 April, with renewed fighting in May and August 1979 and in February 1980; by early 1980 the IRGC had occupied the Turkmen towns. The councils did not secede, and control of towns flipped; included for completeness at low confidence.

control.controller_note: Sheikh Ubeydullah of Nehri and his Kurdish tribal host (Ottoman and Iranian Kurds) vs. Qajar forces from Tabriz
control.note: Tens of thousands of Kurds crossed into north-west Persia in autumn 1880, took Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh, failed to take Urmia (its Shia population refused to surrender) and withdrew after about eight weeks. Exact start/end dates not fixed in the sources consulted. Wikipedia ('Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah') says Ubeydullah's son Abdulqadir 'retreated to Mahabad, which they held for a few days' before Qajar forces from Tabriz arrived, and that after about eight weeks the rebels retreated; Urmia held out. Control was transient and set up no administration, so it is shown as contested (low confidence).

cites.note: cross-check; ~8 weeks, Mahabad and Maragheh taken, Urmia held out
cross-check; Mahabad held a few days; withdrawal after eight weeks

control.controller_note: Assyrian/Armenian forces, Simko's Shikak and local Persian notables after Russia's withdrawal
control.note: Russian troops left Azerbaijan between Jan and March 1918. Simko murdered the Assyrian patriarch Mar Shimun on 3 March 1918; Assyrians, Armenians and Kurds fought for the Urmia plain until the Ottomans arrived. Control was fragmented and short-lived.

control.controller_note: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
control.note: Dilman (Salmas) fell on 18 June and Urmia on 31 July 1918; Ottoman forces left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918).

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

control.controller_note: United Kingdom (Persia and Iraq Force), later joined by the US Persian Gulf Command (from Dec 1942) in Khuzestan
control.note: British forces entered Khuzestan, took Abadan and the Ahvaz oilfields and advanced from Iraq via Kermanshah to Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941. Iranian administration continued. The Allies withdrew from Tehran on 17 Oct 1941; British (and US) troops left by 2 March 1946 under the Tripartite Treaty.

control.controller_note: Soviet Union (44th and 47th Armies)
control.note: Soviet troops took Tabriz and Ardabil by 26 Aug 1941. Iranian civil administration continued; the Tripartite Treaty (29 Jan 1942) declared the presence not an occupation and required withdrawal within six months of the end of hostilities (2 March 1946).

control.controller_note: Azerbaijan People's Government (Democratic Party of Azerbaijan; Ja'far Pishevari, premier) under Soviet protection
control.note: The Democrats took Tabriz around 20-21 Nov 1945 and proclaimed the Autonomous Government of Azerbaijan on 12 Dec 1945 while Soviet troops blocked the Iranian army. Soviet forces left in May 1946; Iranian forces began moving in on 9 Dec 1946 and entered Tabriz on 12-13 Dec 1946, when Pishevari fled to Baku. Dating: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') says all major routes into the province were seized by the Democrats by 19 Nov 1945, an Iranian column of 1,500 troops was stopped at Qazvin by the Soviets, and Tabriz was 'in the hands of the Democratic Party' by 10 Dec 1945; Wikipedia has 21 Nov. The Soviet-held zone therefore reached the Qazvin line. Zanjan province is included on the strength of general accounts; Iranica does not name it (the Iranian advance of Dec 1946 is said to have moved on Zanjan, but no source was found here).

control.controller_note: Soviet Union (based at Mashhad and Bojnurd)
control.note: Soviet troops entered Khorasan on 3 Shahrivar 1320 (25 Aug 1941) from Sarakhs, Dargaz and Bajgiran and occupied the north-east, based at Mashhad and Bojnurd; Iranian civil administration continued. Iranica ('Khorasan xi') says the Soviets stayed 'until the winter of 1943', but the Soviet communique of 25 Feb 1946 announced that evacuation of 'Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan' would begin on 2 March 1946, and on 24-25 March the Soviets (via Kennan, FRUS) said it 'has already been finished' (Mossadegh doubted this on 3-4 March). 'Winter of 1943' is probably a mis-conversion of winter 1324 Sh. (1945-46). The end date is the Soviet claim of completion; the south-east (Birjand, Tabas) was not in the Soviet zone.

cites.note: Soviet statement that evacuation of Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan, begun 2 Mar 1946, was finished

control.controller_note: Soviet Union
control.note: Soviet forces took Gilan (Anzali, Rasht), Mazandaran and Gorgan in August 1941 and reached Qazvin; they entered Tehran on 17 Sept 1941 and withdrew from it by 17 Oct. Iranian civil administration continued. The last Soviet troops left on about 6-9 May 1946. Semnan province, evacuated by 24 March 1946, is mapped separately.

control.controller_note: Baluch chiefs of Sarhad (Rigi, Ismailzai, Damani, Baranzai) who had come to terms with the Persian governor of Bampur; Persian officials at Bampur, Khash and Nasratabad
control.note: Gazetteer of Persia vol. IV (c.1908-10): the power of the Sarhad chiefs 'continued almost undiminished', although 'within the last few years' they had submitted to the Persian governor of Bampur, and a small Persian party from Bampur, Khash or Nasratabad could pass through Sarhad levying taxes or blackmail on chiefs and headmen. That is acknowledgment of the shah's governor by local chiefs (indirect), not a total absence of state authority. Koyagi: Qajar presence 'waned significantly' after 1906, leaving a vacuum that raiding exploited. The 1850-1900 stretch is weakly documented (Persian garrison at Bampur from 1850) and may have been 'none'; the status shown is a low-confidence compromise. Frontier demarcated 1895-96.

control.controller_note: Soviet Union
control.note: Soviet forces held Semnan province (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan) on the Tehran-Mashhad route from the August 1941 invasion; Iranian civil administration continued. Evacuation of Shahrud and Semnan began on 2 March 1946 and was reported finished by 24-25 March (FRUS 1946 VII, doc. 282). Split from the other Soviet-held provinces, which were evacuated until about 6-9 May 1946.

cites.note: Soviet statement that evacuation of Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan, begun 2 Mar 1946, was finished

control.controller_note: Imperial Russian army (Gen. Paskevich)
control.note: Khoy was held as a deposit until the whole indemnity was paid. Kinneir's letters show the Russians still in Khoy on 14 and 25 Aug 1828 (he suspected they hoped to occupy it indefinitely), and his dispatch of 26 Nov 1828 reports the withdrawal from Khoy in exchange for a large Persian payment (with a 100,000-toman gift from Paskevich on receipt). End set to Nov 1828 (low); the start month is not established (after the fall of Tabriz on 13 Oct 1827).

control.controller_note: Qashqai ilkhani family (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan), reinstated in the Majles after the truce
control.note: After the 1929 truce Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were reinstated as deputies, the military governors were withdrawn from tribal territory and a general amnesty was declared (Iranica). The Qashqai rebelled again in 1932 'but in vain', Soulat al-Dowleh died in prison in 1933 and the army then cut the migration routes; direct control followed. Low confidence on both ends.

control.controller_note: Pro-German officers of the Fars Gendarmerie and Democrat Party members (with the Tangestani khans and the German agent Wassmuss as allies)
control.note: On 10 Nov 1915 the Gendarmerie seized the government buildings of Shiraz and arrested the British consul (Maj. O'Connor) and the British colony, having 'openly declared with the Germans and revolted against their own Government' (India Office file); Iranica places the expulsion of the British-backed acting governor Habib-Allah Qavam al-Molk in late 1915. His son Ebrahim Khan Qavam al-Molk, with a British-aided tribal army and pro-British gendarmes, took the city back in April 1916 and became acting governor-general. Gendarmes also seized Kerman and Yazd in the same crisis according to Wikipedia, but without dates; not mapped. Rebel-held for about five months.

control.controller_note: Babis led by Mulla Mohammad-'Ali Hojjat al-Eslam Zanjani (about 2,000 fighters and their families) vs. the governor and the shah's army
control.note: The Zanjan 'upheaval' began on 13 May 1850; from about 19 May the town was divided in two, with the Babis holding their fortified quarters against the governor and then against the army that gathered from June (Aziz Khan Mokri, commander-in-chief, arrived on 25 Aug). Hojjat died on 29 Dec and the last Babi positions fell in a general assault about 2 Jan 1851. An eight-month armed enclave, shown as contested because the town was split rather than ceded to a separate government. The Babi stand at Shaykh Tabarsi (Mazandaran, late 1848-May 1849) and the Neyriz rising (1850) were also armed enclaves but were not mapped (single fort / weeks).

cites.note: 13 May 1850 - 2 Jan 1851; low-grade source, cross-check only

control.controller_note: Imperial Russia (Cossack and line garrisons at Urmia, Khoy and Salmas)
control.note: Wikipedia ('Persian campaign (World War I)') says Russia occupied Tabriz in 1909 and Urmia and Khoy in 1910 to secure the road from Julfa to Van; Russian consulates and garrisons controlled the Urmia plain until the Russian withdrawal of Jan-Mar 1918. In Dec 1914 the Russians pulled back to one brigade around Salmas and Urmia and the Ottomans held Urmia from 4 Jan 1915 and briefly Salmas/Dilman; the Russians returned from early Feb 1915 (the Tabriz record treats the same break as under two months). Persian civil administration continued. Start month and extent are approximate (Salmas on the strength of the 1915 fighting at Dilman).

cites.note: cross-check; Russian occupation of Urmia and Khoy in 1910; Dec 1914 withdrawal; Jan-Mar 1915

control.controller_note: British Indian Army (Indian Expeditionary Force D, 6th Poona Division) guarding the Anglo-Persian Oil Company refinery
control.note: On 6 Nov 1914, the day after Britain's war with the Ottoman Empire began, Indian Expeditionary Force D occupied Fao and then Abadan island, where Sheikh Khaz'al (who rented the island to the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in 1909 and administered it until 1924) allowed the British to garrison the refinery; a small force went up the Karun to Ahvaz in Feb-Mar 1915 (Battle of Ahvaz, 3 Mar 1915). The withdrawal date is unknown; the Armistice of November 1918 is used. Treated as foreign occupation despite the sheikh's consent, like the Bushehr and SPR records.

cites.note: cross-check; IEF D occupies Fao and Abadan, 6 Nov 1914

control.controller_note: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
control.note: Sykes's column reached Kerman on 12 June 1916 and an SPR brigade was stationed there by December 1916; Persian civil governors remained and the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. Same caveat as the Bandar Abbas record (assented under pressure).

control.controller_note: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
control.note: Sykes marched into Shiraz on 11 Nov 1916 with the new governor-general Farman Farma (Iranica 'Fars iv'); an SPR brigade stayed there until the force was disbanded in 1921. Persian civil governors remained; same caveat as the other SPR records.

events.title: Qajar-era lease of Bandar Abbas and the Minab-Khamir coast to Muscat
events.summary: Under a Persian firman of 1793 (lease of 1794) the Sultan of Muscat administered Bandar Abbas, the coast from Minab to Khamir and the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz for 75 years. The arrangement was contested in 1804-10 by Mulla Hosein of Qeshm and the Qawasim and was restricted to 20 years from 1855.

events.title: Russian troops enter Tbilisi
events.summary: Russian troops entered Tbilisi following the Georgievsk protectorate (1783) and the 1795 Persian sack, ending Iranian leverage over Kartli-Kakheti ahead of formal annexation.

events.title: Paul I decrees annexation of Kartli-Kakheti
events.summary: Decree of 18 Dec 1800 OS annexing the kingdom; confirmed by Alexander I (Manifesto of 12 Sept 1801 OS = 24 Sept NS; Iranica gives 21 Sept). Tehran never recognised it; renunciation only at Gulistan.

events.title: Talysh khan accepts Russian protection
events.summary: Mir Mostafa Khan of Talysh accepted Russian protection (1802 per Wikipedia), starting a decade of contested control of the Lankaran lowland.

events.title: Qajars retake Mashhad from Nader Mirza Afshar
events.summary: After failed attempts in 1799 and 1801 and a personal campaign in 1802, Fath-Ali Shah's forces under Mohammad-Vali Mirza entered Mashhad in early 1803. Nader Mirza was taken to Tehran and executed; Khorasan came under Qajar control, though local khans kept wide autonomy.

events.title: Russians storm Ganja
events.summary: Tsitsianov stormed Ganja (3 Jan 1804 OS), killing Javad Khan; renamed Elisavetpol, the khanate abolished 1805. Opened the first Russo-Persian war.

events.title: Shaki, Shirvan and Shuragel accept Russian suzerainty (1805-Jan 1806)
events.summary: Salim Khan of Shaki and the Shuragel sultan submitted in 1805; Mostafa Khan of Shirvan formally renounced Persian vassalage on 6 Jan 1806 NS (25 Dec 1805 OS, treaty at the foot of Fit-Dagh). Shaki later abolished 1819, Shirvan 1820.

events.title: Treaty of Kurakchay (Karabakh)
events.summary: Ibrahim Khalil Khan of Karabakh accepted Russian suzerainty (14 May 1805 OS = 26 May NS); Russian garrison at Shusha. Khan killed by Russian soldiers 2 June 1806; Mehdi Qoli installed.

events.title: Russians occupy Quba
events.summary: Quba occupied by Bulgakov after Derbent and Baku (1806); Shaykh Ali Khan fled.

events.title: Russians take Derbent
events.summary: Derbent's citizens rebelled against Shaykh Ali Khan and invited General Glazenap; the naib handed over the keys on 3 July 1806 NS (21 June OS). Bulgakov then moved on Baku (taken Oct 1806) and Quba.

events.title: Fall of Baku (after Tsitsianov's death)
events.summary: Tsitsianov was shot outside Baku on 20 Feb 1806 (8 Feb OS); the Russians captured Baku in Oct 1806 (3 Oct OS = 15 Oct NS; Wikipedia says 6 Oct). Hosein Qoli Khan fled to Ardabil.

events.title: Persian expedition to Herat (Shahdih)
events.summary: Fath-Ali Shah's forces defeated Firuz al-Din Mirza (battle of Shahdih, 1807); tribute exacted and Persian suzerainty (claimed since c.1801) reasserted, repeated 1814.

events.title: Lankaran stormed
events.summary: Kotlyarevsky stormed Lankaran (1 Jan 1813 OS); Mir Mostafa Khan fled. Russia held the Lankaran lowland at the armistice.

events.title: Treaty of Gulistan
events.summary: Signed 12 Oct OS (24 Oct NS; Iranica: 29 Shawwal 1228) at Gulistan; ratified at Tbilisi Sept 1814. Persia recognised Russian sovereignty over Georgia (with Shuragel), Daghestan, Karabakh, Ganja, Shaki, Shirvan, Derbent, Quba, Baku and Talysh (frontier left to commissioners), and Russian-held lands generally. Gokcha/Sevan and Erivan stayed Persian; the vague frontier fuelled the 1826 war. Art. II line: 'Adinabazar - straight through Mugan lowland - Yeddibulag passage - up to the joint of the river Kapanak with Araz - Mehri chain - boundaries of Karabakh and Nakhchivan khanates - Alagoz - boundary of Daralayaz - Iravan/Yelizavetpol, Gazakh and Shamsaddin lands - Pambak mountains - boundary of Shuragol - Arpachay'; the Talysh frontier 'at Zinzeley and Ardabil' was left to commissioners (Ermolov's 1818 commission). Art. III: 'Karabakh khanate and Yelizavetpol province (former Ganja khanate), the khanates of Sheki, Shirvan, Derbend, Guba, Baku and Talish..., Dagestan, Georgia (together with the province of Shuragol), Imperiya, Guriya, Mingrelia and Abkhaziya'. Signed 12 Oct OS = 24 Oct NS (29 Shawwal 1228); IBS 25 gives 12 Oct 1813, ratified at Tiflis 15 Sept 1814.

events.title: Barakzai coup in Herat
events.summary: Fath Khan Barakzai deposed Firuz al-Din (April 1818); the Sadozai Mahmud and Kamran then ruled Herat independently of Tehran.

events.title: Ottoman-Persian war
events.summary: Abbas Mirza crossed at Gurbulak (16 Sept 1821), stormed Bayezid in Nov 1821 and beat the Ottomans at Toprakkale (May 1822); Mohammad Ali Mirza took Shahrizor and Sulaymaniyah and besieged Baghdad until he died of cholera on 22 Nov 1822.

events.title: Bruce-Farmanfarma agreement on Bahrain
events.summary: Resident William Bruce and Fars governor Hosein Ali Mirza Farmanfarma agreed that Bahrain was 'always subordinate to the province of Fars'; London disowned it, Tehran cited it for a century.

events.title: First Treaty of Erzurum
events.summary: Restored the status quo ante bellum (1639 Zuhab / 1746 frontier); Persia evacuated Bayezid and Shahrizor; Persian pilgrims' access guaranteed.

events.title: Russia occupies north shore of Lake Gokcha
events.summary: Yermolov seized the northern bank of Lake Gokcha (Sevan) in early 1825, claiming Gulistan allowed it; Iran protested and the occupation became the main grievance behind the 1826 war. The Russian war manifesto conceded Persia's right to the district.

events.title: Russo-Persian war reopens; Persian counter-offensive
events.summary: Abbas Mirza's army crossed the Aras in July 1826 (Russia took Bash-Aparan on 8 July; Persia took Pambak/Shuragel late July). Local uprisings in Talysh, Shirvan, Ganja and elsewhere helped Persia retake most Gulistan-ceded lands in summer 1826. Because Tehran had renounced these lands in 1813, they are mapped as 'iranian_held', not as restored claims, although the war's aim was to reverse Gulistan.

events.title: Mir Hasan Khan and Qajar troops retake Lankaran
events.summary: After six days' fighting from 25 July 1826 OS the Russian garrison abandoned Lankaran (31 July OS = 12 Aug NS); Iranian forces also took Salyan. Mir Hasan Khan then held Talysh in the shah's name until Turkmenchay (Tapper 1997); a Russian recapture of the coast later in 1826-27 is asserted in Wikipedia's 'Mir-Hasan Khan' but has no date or primary source.

events.title: Battle of Shamkhor; Ganja retaken
events.summary: Madatov routed the Persian vanguard at Shamkhor (3-4 Sept OS = 15-16 Sept NS) and re-entered Ganja about 17 Sept, ending Persian possession of Ganja. Shusha had withstood a siege begun about 6 Aug.

events.title: Battle of Ganja (Elisavetpol); Persians withdraw across the Aras
events.summary: Paskevich-era counterattack: Abbas Mirza's army was beaten at Elisavetpol on 13 Sept OS (25 Sept NS) and retreated across the Aras, abandoning Karabakh.

events.title: Battle of Javad; Shirvan lost again
events.summary: Mishchenko defeated Mostafa Khan and Persian regulars; Shirvan, which had gone over to Mostafa Khan about 4 Aug, returned to Russia.

events.title: Echmiadzin surrenders; blockade of Erivan
events.summary: Paskevich took Echmiadzin in April 1827 and invested Erivan, raising the siege in July to turn on Nakhchivan.

events.title: Russians occupy Nakhchivan
events.summary: Paskevich's detachment entered Nakhchivan without a fight in early July 1827 (some sources give 26 May); Abbas Mirza retreated. Exact day uncertain.

events.title: Abbasabad fortress surrenders
events.summary: Ehsan Khan Kangarlu opened the gates of Abbasabad (built 1810 by Abbas Mirza at Yazdabad on the northern bank of the Aras, c.6 miles SW of Nakhchivan) after the Russians failed to storm it on 14 July and began a siege (Iranica: 27 Dhu'l-Hijja 1242 = 22 July 1827; Russian-based accounts: 7 July OS = 19 July NS).

events.title: Russians occupy Ordubad
events.summary: Russian columns reached Ordubad on 1 Aug 1827 OS (13 Aug NS); the Persian governor withdrew behind the Aras.

events.title: Fall of Erivan
events.summary: After Sardarabad fell, Paskevich took the Erivan citadel on 1 Oct 1827 OS (13 Oct NS; Wikipedia's text says 14 Oct). Tabriz followed 24 Oct.

events.title: Russian army occupies Tabriz, Urmia and Ardabil
events.summary: Paskevich took Tabriz (13 Oct 1827), Urmia (28 Jan 1828) and Ardabil (8 Feb 1828). Under Turkmenchay (22 Feb 1828) Russia kept Azerbaijan as security for the 10-kurur indemnity; most of it was evacuated by about April 1828 (Kinneir, 12 Mar 1828), but Khoy was held as a deposit until about November 1828 (Kinneir, Aug and Nov 1828).

cites.note: cross-check; Tabriz 13 Oct 1827, Urmia 28 Jan 1828, Ardabil 8 Feb 1828
Paskevich leaving Tabriz, evacuation of Khoy tied to indemnity instalments

events.title: Treaty of Turkmenchay
events.summary: Signed 10 Feb 1828 OS (22 Feb NS; Persian date 5 Sha'ban 1243 = 21 Feb) by Abbas Mirza and Asef al-Dowleh. Persia ceded the Erivan and Nakhchivan khanates (Art. 3, incl. Ordubad) and the remainder of Talysh/Mughan; frontier on the Aras, a semicircular Russian bridgehead on the right bank at Abbasabad (held to 1893) and the Astara river to the Caspian (Art. 4); indemnity of 10 kurur (million tomans). Art. IV line: Ararat peak - Ashagi Garasu - Aras to the tower of Abbasgala (a circle of 1.5 versts radius on the right bank stays Russian) - Yeddibulag - Mugan lowland - Bolgarchay - Adinabazar - Cikoir highland - mountains separating Talish from Arsh - chain separating Zuvand and Arsh ('the region of Zuvand is joined to Russia') - north source of the Astara - down the Astara to the Caspian. Hijri 5 Sha'ban 1243 converts to 21 Feb 1828; the Russian Old Style date 10 Feb = 22 Feb NS is used.

events.title: Qajar expeditions to Sarakhs, Khwarazm and the Turkmen
events.summary: Abbas Mirza led an expedition to Sarakhs and Khwarazm in 1832, and Mohammad Shah another in 1837 (Iranica: Persia asserted claims to Marv, Khiva and Sarakhs). Khiva/Khwarazm was claimed rhetorically but no sustained claim or administration is documented, so it is not mapped.

events.title: Abbas Mirza captures Mohammad Khan Qara'i; end of the Qara'i principality
events.summary: Crown Prince Abbas Mirza took Mohammad Khan Qara'i of Torbat-e Heydarieh by deception in 1832; Qajar appointees governed Torbat thereafter.

events.title: Abbas Mirza's Herat campaign ends
events.summary: Abbas Mirza's army besieged Herat in 1832-33; he died Oct 1833 and his son withdrew after a late-Nov 1833 arrangement with Kamran (hostage, coin and khutba in the shah's name, tribute), per Wikipedia.

events.title: Ottoman governor sacks Muhammarah
events.summary: Ali Rida Pasha of Baghdad sacked Muhammarah (Khorramshahr) in 1837, part of the Perso-Ottoman crisis of 1837-43 that led to the Erzurum conference.

events.title: Treaty between Mohammad Shah and the Kandahar sardars
events.summary: The Kandahar sardars (Kohandil Khan) accepted Persian suzerainty during the Herat campaign; Russian diplomacy encouraged the Tehran-Kandahar-Kabul entente. Date and terms not found in detail.

events.title: Ottoman capture of Muhammara by Ali Rida Pasha
events.summary: The Ottoman governor of Baghdad invaded the Ka'b sheikhdom of Muhammara, captured and destroyed the town and received the sheikhs' homage; the town was then alternately claimed and held by Persia and the Ottomans until 1847. How long the Ottoman occupation lasted in 1837 is not established.

cites.note: cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum

events.title: Siege of Herat (Mohammad Shah)
events.summary: Siege from 23/24 Nov 1837, lasting nearly ten months; the shah withdrew empty-handed on 9 Sept 1838 under British pressure (Kharg occupied).

events.title: Russia founds a naval station on Ashurada
events.summary: After a 1838 Persian request for help against Turkmen raiders, Russia built barracks and stationed warships on Ashurada in Gorgan Bay (Iranica 'Ashurada'; other dates: 1837, 1841). Russia recognised Persian sovereignty but refused to leave until the Persian-Soviet treaty of February 1921.

events.title: British occupation of Kharg Island (first)
events.summary: Britain occupied Kharg on 19 June 1838 as a response to Mohammad Shah's siege of Herat and moved its Residency there from Bushehr. The island was held until March 1842 because of Persian diplomatic evasions.

events.title: Persian siege of Herat lifted
events.summary: Mohammad Shah lifted the siege on 9 Sept 1838 after the British occupation of Kharg and McNeill's ultimatum.

events.title: British occupy Kandahar
events.summary: The Army of the Indus entered Kandahar (25 April 1839), ending the Barakzai principality's independence.

events.title: Persia relinquishes claims on Kandahar
events.summary: A treaty with the Kandahar chief is reported (India Office Military Report on Persia) to have ended Persian claims to Afghan territory; low confidence, no text seen.

events.title: Second Treaty of Erzurum
events.summary: Negotiated 19-31 May 1847 (British and Russian mediation). Persia renounced all claim to Sulaymaniyah and ceded the western Zohab lowlands; the Ottomans gave up the eastern mountains and Kirind valley and recognised Persian Muhammarah (Khorramshahr), Khizr (Abadan) island, the anchorage and the east bank; the Shatt al-Arab itself stayed Ottoman with Persian free navigation.

cites.note: cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum

events.title: Mashhad rises for Hasan Khan Salar
events.summary: Mashhad's residents and ulama massacred officials and soldiers on 25 Aug 1848, just before Mohammad Shah's death, and Salar made the shrine city the centre of a revolt that had begun in northern Khorasan in 1846-47. Hamza Mirza's army withdrew and Salar dominated most of Khorasan.

cites.note: cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology

events.title: Persian troops occupy Bampur
events.summary: Persian forces occupied Bampur in 1849 and garrisoned it permanently in 1850; the local rulers of Dizzak, Sarbaz, Geh and Qasr-e Qand then accepted the obligation to pay taxes to the governor, Ebrahim Khan. Before this Persian Baluchistan was "practically independent".

events.title: Mashhad surrenders; Hasan Khan Salar executed
events.summary: Sultan Morad Mirza retook Sabzevar (9 March 1849) and Neyshabur (21 March 1849) and besieged Mashhad from June 1849; the city surrendered on 13 or 23 March 1850 and Salar, his son and brother were executed on 29 April 1850.

cites.note: cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology

events.title: Babi uprising at Zanjan
events.summary: Hojjat Zanjani's Babi followers held part of Zanjan against the governor and the shah's army from 13 May 1850 until a general assault about 2 Jan 1851 killed several hundred.

events.title: Persian army takes Herat
events.summary: Hesam o-Saltaneh's army, with French engineers, captured Herat (11 or 25 Oct 1856; ceremonial entry 30 Oct). Britain declared war 1 Nov 1856 and landed at Bushehr.

events.title: Anglo-Persian War: British take Kharg and Bushehr
events.summary: British naval forces occupied Kharg on 4 Dec 1856, stormed Reshire on 5 Dec and took Bushehr on 9-10 Dec 1856; Borazjan was occupied on 5 Feb 1857 and the Battle of Khushab was fought on 8 Feb.

events.title: Treaty of Paris (Anglo-Persian)
events.summary: Signed 4 March 1857 (ratified 2 May at Baghdad). Art. V: evacuate Herat within three months; Art. VI: Persia relinquishes all claims to Herat and Afghanistan and any tribute, coin or khutba, and accepts British good offices in disputes.

events.title: British take Mohammerah and reach Ahvaz
events.summary: After a naval bombardment Mohammerah fell on 26-27 March 1857 and an armed flotilla reached Ahvaz on 1 April; the Treaty of Paris (signed 4 March, ratified 2 May 1857) ended the war.

events.title: British evacuate Mohammerah, Bushehr and Kharg
events.summary: The main British force left the Gulf in mid-1857 (May-June, because of the Indian Mutiny); Bushehr was evacuated in October 1857 (Wikipedia) and Kharg held until spring 1858 (Iranica). Exact dates by place are not firmly established.

events.title: Persian troops leave Herat
events.summary: Persian garrison evacuated by about Sept 1857 after installing Sultan Ahmad Khan in April; Dost Mohammad took Herat 27 May 1863.

events.title: Disastrous Persian Merv expedition
events.summary: The 1860-61 campaign against Merv (Hesam al-Saltaneh) ended in a crushing defeat, 'the beginning of the end of Iran's claims to dominion over the Khavaran plain'.

events.title: Tehran claims all Makran and Baluchistan
events.summary: In 1281 AH (1864) Iran officially claimed all Makran and Baluchistan, grounding it in Nader Shah's 1736 conquest.

events.title: Persian takeover of western Sistan
events.summary: Persian invasion of Sistan in 1865 with a governor (Hesmat-al-Molk); Persia had been reclaiming Sistan since 1772. Western Sistan, inside modern Iran, is shown in its own region.

events.title: Naser al-Din Shah abolishes the Ardalan vilayet
events.summary: In 1284/1867-68 the shah ended Kurdistan's special status as a semi-autonomous frontier province and appointed his uncle Farhad Mirza Mo'tamed al-Dowleh governor, ending Ardalan rule.

events.title: Persia regains Bandar Abbas from Muscat
events.summary: After the expulsion of Sayyid Salim bin Thuwaini from Muscat (October 1868) the lease became void; Persia appointed Haji Ahmad, formerly Salim's minister, to govern Bandar Abbas and its dependencies.

events.title: Russo-Persian agreement on the Atrek
events.summary: Russia recognised the Atrek as the boundary (about 30 miles east of the Caspian); Persia dropped claims north of it.

events.title: Goldsmid's Perso-Kalat line
events.summary: Notes exchanged 1 and 4 Sept 1871 (Alison for Kalat; Mirza Saeed Khan) fixed the line from Kuhak to Gwatar Bay, leaving Panjgur, Kohuk, Buleda, Mand/Tump/Kech and Dasht with Kalat; Britain kept treating Gwadar as Omani.

events.title: Goldsmid's Sistan arbitration
events.summary: Award (1872) split Sistan along the Helmand, giving Persia 'Seistan proper' and Afghanistan the right bank; accepted by both governments in spring 1873. McMahon's 1903-05 award re-fixed it after the river shifted; Persia's shah protested but the award was accepted.

events.title: Iran reclaims Kuhak after the 1871 line
events.summary: The notes of 1 and 4 Sept 1871 (Alison for Kalat; Mirza Saeed Khan) placed the small district of Kohuk on the Kalat side. In 1872 a joint Anglo-Iranian commission examined the line; Iran then claimed Kuhak and the British agreed the line should lie east of it. Iran occupied Kuhak in May 1874. The exact date of the renewed claim (1872-74) is not documented.

events.title: Goldsmid arbitration awards west Sistan to Persia
events.summary: The British arbitration mission under Col. Goldsmid divided Sistan: the lands west of the Helmand were awarded to Persia and the right bank to Afghanistan. Sistanis rebelled against the Qa'en chief later that year and Persian governors followed in 1873.

events.title: Persian forces expel an Omani claimant from Chahbar
events.summary: 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of the Sultan of Muscat, seized Chahbar in January 1872; a Persian army expelled him in March (the governor of Bampur, Sartip Ebrahim Khan, had asserted Persian ownership), ending Oman's hold.

events.title: Iran occupies Kuhak
events.summary: Iran occupied Kuhak in May 1874 after claiming it despite the 1871 line.

events.title: Treaty of Berlin Art. LX: Turkey to cede Kotur
events.summary: Art. LX obliged Turkey to cede the Kotur territory to Persia; the Sary Kamish protocol (15 July OS = 27 July NS 1880) delimited it but the Ottomans did not implement the cession for decades (Kotur remained disputed until the 1932 agreement).

events.title: Sheikh Ubeydullah's invasion of north-west Persia
events.summary: In the last months of 1880 tens of thousands of Ottoman and Iranian Kurds under Sheikh Ubeydullah of Nehri took control of Sauj Bulaq and Maragheh and ravaged villages around Urmia; Urmia held out and the host withdrew after about eight weeks.

cites.note: cross-check; ~8 weeks, Mahabad and Maragheh taken, Urmia held out

events.title: Akhal-Khorasan convention fixes the Russo-Persian frontier in the Turkmen steppe
events.summary: Following the Russian conquest of the Akhal Teke, the 1299/1881 convention effectively ended Iran's claims to Marv and the Turkmen steppe; the Yomut and Goklen within Persia thereafter dealt with a Russian-bordered Persian state. (Frontier effects are for the frontier layer.)

events.title: Russians storm Geok Tepe
events.summary: Fall of the Tekke fortress (12 Jan 1881 OS) ended Akhal independence.

events.title: Akhal-Khorasan Convention
events.summary: Convention of 9/21 Dec 1881 (Wikipedia gives 21 Sept) set the frontier east of the Caspian to Babadurmaz and ended Iran's claims beyond the Tejen (Marv, Abivard, Nesa, Meyhana); Firyuza left to Persia.

events.title: Russia expels Persian garrison from Old Sarakhs
events.summary: Komarov's Russians annexed Merv in 1884 and took Old Sarakhs on the Hari Rud in 1884-85; Persia's claim there ended with the 1893 convention.

events.title: Persia takes Sirri and ends the Qasimi deputy-governorship of Lengeh
events.summary: In Feb 1887 Persia merged the ports of Bushehr, Lengeh and Bandar Abbas with their dependent districts and islands into the 'Persian Gulf Ports' administration; in Sept 1887 it dissolved the Qasimi deputy governorship of Lengeh and four days later landed a 30-man garrison, two cannon and a flagstaff on Sirri. Britain decided in Aug 1888 tacitly to acquiesce.

events.title: Persia ends Qasimi rule at Bandar Lengeh
events.summary: In February 1887 Persia created the "Gulf Ports" governorate (Bushehr, Lengeh, Bandar Abbas); in September the Qasimi governorship of Lengeh was dissolved, Sheikh Qazib was arrested and sent to Tehran and a Persian garrison landed. A 1898-99 interlude under Sheikh Mohammad ibn Khalifa ended when Ahmad Khan Daryabeigi retook the town in March 1899.

events.title: First documented Persian claim to Abu Musa
events.summary: A report prepared by the Persian military 'for use by the prime minister' claimed Abu Musa; Britain neither countered nor objected. Copies of a British War Office map showing the islands as Persian were presented to the Shah in July 1888.

events.title: MacLean arbitration (Hashtadan)
events.summary: Hashtadan plain dispute began Mar 1885 when Persians began to cultivate it; MacLean (1888-91) fixed a compromise line from the Hari Rud south to pillar 39 (c. 34 deg 20'N, 60 deg 55'E) with a deflection round Hashtadan mound. Not mapped as a region (extent not found).

events.title: Convention for territorial interchange (Tehran)
events.summary: Signed 27 May OS (8 June NS) 1893: Persia ceded the Firyuza oasis and district; Russia gave up the Abbasabad bridgehead and the Hissar oasis near Lotfabad, and the frontier east of Babadurmaz to Afghanistan was delimited. Hissar is not mapped because its extent is uncertain.

events.title: Holdich line (Kuhak to Malik Siah)
events.summary: Agreement of 27 Dec 1895, proces-verbal of 24 March 1896 and demarcation agreement of 26 March 1896 formally included Kuhak in Iran; 11 pillars to Gorani. Boundary beyond pillar 11 left open.

events.title: Khaz'al becomes Sheikh of Mohammerah
events.summary: Khaz'al Khan succeeded his assassinated brother Mazal as sheikh of Mohammerah in June 1897 and built a semi-independent realm in Khuzestan under British protection.

events.title: Competing flag-raising on the Tunbs and Abu Musa
events.summary: July 1903: the British Resident had the shaikh of Sharjah plant his flag on Greater Tonb to pre-empt a Persian move; March 1904: a Persian customs contingent landed, removed the Sharjah flags, raised the Persian standard and posted two riflemen at each site (a Belgian customs official in Persian service is named in some accounts); 14 June 1904: Persia withdrew 'subject to the reservations' (the 'status quo agreement'); the Tunbs were then administered by Sharjah (1904-21) and Ras al-Khaimah (1921-71).

events.title: McMahon Sistan arbitration
events.summary: McMahon's award (Nov 1903) fixed the Helmand/Nad Ali line; 90 pillars placed by 15 May 1905. Accepted by Afghanistan; Mozaffar al-Din Shah protested from Europe but the line stands.

events.title: Ottoman encroachments on Persian border districts
events.summary: From about 1905 to 1912 Ottoman troops repeatedly occupied Persian frontier districts (reported at Urmia/Sauj Bulaq, Zohab/Mehran and Kotur; details are thin); the 21 Dec 1911 Tehran frontier agreement set up the commission that produced the 1913 Protocol. The occupied districts inside modern Iran are shown as their own region.

events.title: Anglo-Iranian agreement on Mirjaveh
events.summary: The UK withdrew its claim to Mirjaveh; Iran allowed the British post at Padaha to take water.

events.title: Ottoman troops occupy Persian frontier districts
events.summary: Beginning 23 May 1906 at Behik in Baradost, Ottoman troops occupied Dasht, Mergever, Sardasht and other districts from south-west of Sauj Bulaq to west of Khoy, collected taxes near Urmia and re-occupied Mergever on 3 Aug 1907. Russian and British pressure and a frontier commission pushed them back around 1911-12.

events.title: Tabriz resists Mohammad Ali Shah's coup
events.summary: Constitutionalists led by Sattar Khan and Baqer Khan held Tabriz against a royalist siege from the shah's coup (23 June 1908) until Russian troops entered on 30 April 1909.

events.title: Constitutionalists seize Rasht and Isfahan
events.summary: In January 1909 constitutionalist forces took Rasht and Bakhtiari khans took Isfahan; columns from Gilan and Isfahan then marched on Tehran. Months are approximate.

events.title: Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari's revolt in Larestan
events.summary: A pro-constitution mujtahid proclaimed a revolt in 1909, issued his own stamps and, per Iranica, ruled Larestan until spring 1915, when Qavam al-Molk's force sent by the governor-general of Fars pacified it. Continuity of control between 1909 and 1915 is uncertain.

events.title: Russian troops occupy Tabriz (and land at Anzali)
events.summary: On 20 April 1909 Britain, France and Russia agreed to Russian intervention; Gen. Snarski's force occupied Tabriz on 30 April 1909 and Russian troops landed at Anzali and advanced on Qazvin. Russia kept troops in Tabriz, Gilan and Khorasan to 1918.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

events.title: Constitutionalist forces take Tehran
events.summary: Gilani and Bakhtiari columns took Tehran on 13 July 1909 and deposed Mohammad Ali Shah, ending the rebel-held phases at Rasht and Isfahan.

events.title: Salar al-Dowleh's revolt in the west
events.summary: After Mohammad Ali Shah's return attempt, his brother occupied Sanandaj by 17 July 1911 and took Kermanshah and Hamadan with tribal levies; he won near Malayer but was decisively beaten at Saveh by Amir Mofakham Bakhtiari and then held the Kermanshah-Kurdistan area until Farman Farma's 1912 expedition drove him out (he fled in July 1912 to Luristan and Kurdistan). A first revolt in 1907 was routed at Nehavand (Iranica). Mohammad Ali Shah's own July 1911 landing near Astarabad was defeated within weeks and is not mapped. Duration of control of each town is not established.

events.title: Constantinople Protocol
events.summary: Signed 4 Nov OS (17 Nov NS) 1913: detailed delimitation of the whole Turco-Persian frontier except ~40 miles at Kotur. The Shatt al-Arab remained Ottoman except Persian islands near Abadan and the Muhammarah anchorage; Persia evacuated the Zohab 'Transferred Territory'. Persia later challenged its validity.

events.title: Persia hands over the Zohab Transferred Territory
events.summary: Persian forces left the area east of the Sirwan transferred to the Ottomans under the 1913 Protocol; the commission completed demarcation by Oct 1914 except near Kotur.

events.title: Ottoman forces briefly take Urmia and Tabriz
events.summary: Ottoman volunteers took Urmia on 4 Jan 1915 and Kurdish/Ottoman troops entered Tabriz on 8 Jan after the Russian evacuation (17 Dec 1914); Russia re-entered Tabriz on 31 Jan 1915. Under a month, so no region record.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915
cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

events.title: British East Persia Cordon is formed
events.summary: In July 1915 a small force on the Baluchistan frontier became the East Persia Cordon against German infiltration toward Afghanistan; from March 1916 it was the Seistan Force (Dyer from Feb 1916), later extended to Meshed and the Transcaspian line.

cites.note: cross-check; formation July 1915, Seistan Force from March 1916, last elements out Nov 1920

events.title: Tangestani attack on the British Residency at Bushehr
events.summary: Rais Ali Delvari and the Tangestanis, encouraged by the German agent Wassmuss, attacked the Residency on 12 July 1915; the British occupied Bushehr on 8 Aug.

events.title: British occupation of Bushehr
events.summary: British troops took over Bushehr's government on 8 Aug 1915, disarming the gendarmerie; the occupation ended by agreement on 16 Oct 1915, and Persian postal authorities resumed on 18 Oct.

events.title: Kuchek Khan's Jangalis take to the forests of Gilan
events.summary: Mirza Kuchek Khan began the Jangali movement in October 1915 to free Gilan of the Russian army; it later controlled much of Gilan's administration (1917) and survived until December 1921.

events.title: Nationalist government at Kermanshah
events.summary: Nationalists who had left Tehran formed a Committee/National Government at Qom and then Kermanshah (Nezam al-Saltaneh Mafi) allied with the Central Powers; it was driven out by the Russian entry into Kermanshah on 26 Feb 1916, returned with the Ottomans in July 1916 and collapsed in March 1917.

events.title: Pro-German Gendarmerie seizes Shiraz
events.summary: On 10 Nov 1915 the Fars Gendarmerie, aided by Democrat Party radicals, seized Shiraz and arrested the British consul and colony, expelling the British-backed acting governor Qavam al-Molk; the city returned to the Qavam family and the pro-British gendarmes in April 1916 and Sykes's South Persia Rifles arrived in November 1916.

events.title: Baratov's Russian expedition takes Hamadan and Kermanshah
events.summary: The Russian Caucasian Cavalry Corps landed at Anzali (Oct 1915), took Hamadan in December 1915 (3 or 15 Dec) and entered Kermanshah on 26 Feb 1916, then Sanandaj and Bijar on 1-3 March and Qasr-e Shirin in May.

cites.note: cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916
cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

events.title: South Persia Rifles raised and disbanded
events.summary: Sir Percy Sykes landed at Bandar Abbas in March 1916 to raise a British-officered force of up to 11,000 men; brigades sat at Shiraz, Kerman and Bandar Abbas by December 1916; the force was disbanded in 1921 and some personnel entered the new Iranian army.

events.title: Ottoman XIII Corps retakes Kermanshah and Hamadan
events.summary: Ali Ihsan's XIII Corps took Kermanshah on 2 July and Hamadan on 10 Aug 1916, forcing Baratov north; the Ottomans held Kermanshah until the retreat after Baghdad's fall (March 1917).

events.title: Russian troops evacuate Persia
events.summary: After the Bolshevik revolution most Russian troops left Persia between January and March 1918; the last Russians left Tabriz on 28 Feb 1918, while a few under Baratov entered British service.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

events.title: Dunsterforce enters Persia
events.summary: Maj.-Gen. Dunsterville's advance party reached Hamadan in Feb 1918; Dunsterforce held the road from Mesopotamia to Anzali, fought at Manjil (Aug 1918), held Baku 18 Aug-14 Sept and was disbanded on 17 Sept 1918 when Norperforce took over.

events.title: Ottoman reoccupation of Tabriz, Salmas and Urmia
events.summary: Ottoman IV Corps entered Tabriz on 8 June 1918 (another date: 18 June), took Dilman (Salmas) on 18 June and Urmia on 31 July 1918; they withdrew after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918).
